x^3 - 3 x^2 + 6 x - 8.$ If $x=2$ and $x=-\dfrac{4}{3}$ are zeros of $f(x),$ factor $f(x)$ completely." :question/worked-solution "Because $x=2$ and $x=-\dfrac{4}{3}$ are both zeros of $f(x),$ the factor theorem guarantees that $(x-2)$ and $\left( x + \dfrac{4}{3} \right)$ are both factors of $f(x).$ So, $(x-2)$ and $\left( x + \dfrac{4}{3} \right)$ both divide $f(x).$ To begin factoring $f(x),$ we can divide it by one of these factors (it doesn't matter which one we divide first). Let's divide $f(x)$ by $(x-2)$ using synthetic division:
$x^4$ $x^3$ $x^2$ $x^1$ $x^0$
$\color{red}2$ $3$ $-5$ $-3$ $6$ $-8$
$\color{gray}\downarrow$ $6$ $2$ $-2$ $8$
$3$ $1$ $-1$ $4$ $0$
Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned}f(x) & =3{x}^{4}-5{x}^{3}-3{x}^{2}+6x-8 \\ & =(x-2)(3{x}^{3}+{x}^{2}-x+4).\end{aligned} $$ Now, because $\left( x+\dfrac{4}{3} \right)$ is also a factor of $f(x),$ it must be a factor of the quotient $3x^3 + x^2 - x +4.$ So, we divide this quotient by $\left( x+\dfrac{4}{3} \right)$ using synthetic division once more:
$x^3$ $x^2$ $x^1$ $x^0$
$\color{red}-\dfrac{4}{3}$ $3$ $1$ $-1$ $4$
$\color{gray}\downarrow$ $-4$ $4$ $-4$
$3$ $-3$ $3$ $0$
Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned}3{x}^{3}+{x}^{2}-x+4 & =(x+\frac{4}{3})(3{x}^{2}-3x+3) \\ & =(x+\frac{4}{3})(3)({x}^{2}-x+1) \\ & =(3x+4)({x}^{2}-x+1),\end{aligned} $$ which means that $$ \begin{aligned}3{x}^{4}-5{x}^{3}-3{x}^{2}+6x-8 & =(x-2)(3x+4)({x}^{2}-x+1).\end{aligned} $$ The quadratic polynomial $x^2-x+1$ does not appear to factor over the real numbers. We can make sure of this by verifying that its discriminant is negative: $$ \begin{aligned}D={b}^{2}-4ac=(-1)^{2}-4(1)(1)=-3<0\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the full factorization of $f(x)$ over the real numbers is given by $$ f(x) = (x-2)(3x+4)(x^2-x+1). $$"} {:db/id 17592186054580 :question/id #uuid "2a156814-63e0-5686-ac89-2859dbf0d958" :question/math-academy-id "e-76" :question/problem "$$ \displaystyle \lim_{x\to \pi/4}\dfrac{\sin^2{x}-\cos^2{x}}{2\sin{x}\cos{2x}}= $$" :question/worked-solution "If we attempt to evaluate this limit directly, we get an indeterminate form: $$ \begin{aligned} \lim_{x \to π/4}\frac{\sin^{2} x - \cos^{2} x}{2\sin x\cos 2x} &= (\sin^{2} \left(\frac{π}{4}\right) - \cos^{2} \left(\frac{π}{4}\right))/(2\sin \left(\frac{π}{4}\right)\cos (2 \cdot \frac{π}{4})) \\ &= (1 - 1)/(\sqrt{2}\cos \left(\frac{π}{2}\right)) \\ &= \frac{0}{0} \end{aligned} $$ So we need to simplify the expression. The double angle formula for cosine will be useful in this case: $$ \cos{2x}=\cos^2{x}-\sin^2{x} $$ Using the double angle formula above, we have $$ \begin{aligned} \lim_{x \to π/4}\frac{\sin^{2} x - \cos^{2} x}{2\sin x\cos 2x} &= \lim_{x \to π/4}(\sin^{2} x - \cos^{2} x)/(2\sin x(\cos^{2} x - \sin^{2} x)) \\ &= \lim_{x \to π/4}(- (\cos^{2} x - \sin^{2} x))/(2\sin x(\cos^{2} x - \sin^{2} x)) \\ &= \lim_{x \to π/4}\left(-\frac{1}{2\sin x}\right) \\ &=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ &=-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186054583 :question/id #uuid "e656ee8d-55b9-5ea6-beae-7c2caf329a6a" :question/math-academy-id "e-764" :question/problem "The Taylor series for the function $f(x)$ about $x=0$ is given by $$ \displaystyle f(x) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{(-3)^{n}\,x^n}{n^3} $$ The series converges to $f(x)$ for $|x| < R,$ where $R$ is the radius of convergence of the Taylor series. Calculate the radius of convergence of the series expansion of $f'(x),$ the derivative of $f(x),$ about $x=0.$" :question/worked-solution "The radius of convergence for the Taylor series of $f'(x)$ is the same as the Taylor series of $f(x).$ So, to find the radius of convergence of $f'(x),$ we need to compute $R.$ To calculate $R,$ we can use the ratio test. Computing the limit of the absolute value of the ratio of two consecutive terms, we get $$ \begin{aligned}L & =\lim_{n\to \infty }|\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}| \\ & =\lim_{n\to \infty }|\frac{(-3)^{n+1}\,{x}^{n+1}}{(n+1)^{3}}\cdot \frac{{n}^{3}}{(-3)^{n}\,{x}^{n}}| \\ & =\lim_{n\to \infty }|\frac{(-3)x\cdot {n}^{3}}{(n+1)^{3}}| \\ & =3|x|\lim_{n\to \infty }\frac{1}{{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{3}} \\ & =3|x|.\end{aligned} $$ The series converges when $L<1.$ So, it converges when $$ \begin{aligned}3|x| & <1 \\ |x| & <\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the radius of convergence is $R = \dfrac 1 3.$"} {:db/id 17592186054584 :question/id #uuid "b9498461-7676-5414-980e-d9c4bd610aaf" :question/math-academy-id "e-77" :question/problem "Evaluate $$ \displaystyle \lim_{x\to 0}\dfrac{1-\cos x}{3\sin^2\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)}. $$" :question/worked-solution "If we attempt to evaluate this limit directly, we get an indeterminate form: $$ \begin{aligned} \lim_{x \to 0}(1 - \cos x)/(3\sin^{2} \left(\frac{x}{2}\right)) &= (1 - \cos (0))/(3\sin^{2} (0)) \\ &= \frac{1 - 1}{3 \cdot 0} \\ &= \frac{0}{0} \end{aligned} $$ So we need to simplify the expression. In particular, we will use the Pythagorean identity: $$ \cos^2{x}=1-\sin^2{x} $$ Substituting the above formula, we get $$ \begin{aligned} \lim_{x \to (- π/2)}\frac{\cos^{2} x}{1 + \sin x} &= \lim_{x \begin{aligned}9\,\, & \ge \,\,-\frac{x}{4} \\ (-4)\cdot 9\,\, & \le \,\,(-4)\cdot \left(-\frac{x}{4}\right) \\ -36\,\, & \le \,\,(-4)\cdot \left(-\frac{x}{4}\right)\end{aligned} $$ Since two negative \\ -36 & \le 4\cdot \frac{x}{4}\end{aligned} $$ Now, we can cancel the common factor $4$ from both the numerator and denominator. $$ \begin{aligned}-36 & \le 4\cdot \frac{x}{4} \\ -36 & \le \frac{4x}{4} \\ -36 & \le \frac{\cancel{4}x}{\cancel{4}} \\ -36 & \le x\end{aligned} $$ Finally, we rewrite the inequality with the variable on the left-hand side: $$ x\ge -36 $$ Therefore, the solution is $x\ge -36.$"} {:db/id 17592186055052 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "a855e949-709c-5066-9ef9-c7d1d9a2d266" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} {\begin{array}{rl}\displaystyle \lim_{x \to \pi / 2} {\displaystyle \frac{\sin 2 x}{2 \cos x}} & \displaystyle = \lim_{x \to \pi / 2} {\displaystyle \frac{2 \sin x \cos x}{2 \cos x}} \\ \displaystyle \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d} x} ( 2 {x}^{3} ) + \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d} x} ( {y}^{2} ) & = 0 \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d} x} ( 2 {x}^{3} ) + \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d} y} ( {y}^{2} ) ( \frac{\text{d} y}{\text{d} x} ) & = 0 \\ 6 {x}^{2} + 2 y \frac{\text{d} y}{\text{d} x} & = 0\end{array} $$ **Step 2**: Solve the equation for $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}.$ $$ \begin{array}{rl}\displaystyle 6 {x}^{2} + 2 y {\displaystyle \frac{\text{d} y}{\text{d} x}} & \displaystyle = 0 \\ \displaystyle 2 y {\displaystyle \frac{\text{d} y}{\text{d} x}} & \displaystyle = - 6 {x}^{2} \\ \displaystyle {\displaystyle \frac{\text{d} y}{\text{d} x}} & \displaystyle = - {\displaystyle \frac{3 {x}^{2}}{y}}\end{array} $$ So, the derivative of $y$ is $$ \displaystyle \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}=- :question/worked-solution "First, let's interpret the fraction as a division: $$ \dfrac {\cot \theta + \csc \theta} {\cos \theta + 1} = \left(\cot \theta + \csc \theta\right)\div \left(\cos \theta + 1\right) $$ Then, we recall the identities $$ \cot \theta = \dfrac {\cos \theta} {\sin \theta} $$ and $$ \csc\theta = \dfrac{1}{\sin\theta} $$ and we substitute them into the above expression: $$ \begin{aligned} (\cot θ + \csc θ) \div (\cos θ + 1) &= (\frac{\cos θ}{\sin θ} + \frac{1}{\sin θ}) \div (\cos θ + 1) \\ &= \left(\frac{\cos θ + 1}{\sin θ}\right) \div (\cos θ + 1) \end{aligned} $$ Finally, we turn the division into multiplication, and simplify the expression as much as possible: $$ {\begin{array}{rl}\displaystyle ( {\displaystyle \frac{\cos \theta + 1}{\sin \theta }} ) \div ( \cos \theta + 1 ) & \displaystyle = ( {\displaystyle \frac{\cos \theta + 1}{\sin \theta }} ) \cdot ( {\displaystyle \frac{1}{\cos \theta + 1}} ) \\ \displaystyle & \displaystyle = {\displaystyle \frac{\cos \theta + 1}{\sin \theta ( \cos \theta + 1 )}} \\ \displaystyle & \displaystyle = {\displaystyle \frac{\cancel{( \cos \theta + 1 )}}{\sin \theta \cancel{( \cos \theta + 1 )}}} \\ What is $A$?"} {:db/id 17592186060374 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "c71a3a11-3eba-5020-9597-3de35a5ab785" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{7}{6}" :db/id 17592186058867} {:answer/id #uuid "c768ab08-49e9-5e5c-928d-98edae762f8f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{21}{5}" :db/id 17592186058868} {:answer/id #uuid "cf329fcc-fb6f-59d1-adcc-57bc40719b2a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{42}{3}" :db/id 17592186058869} {:answer/id #uuid "22218b3e-4939-5119-bb7f-f0028c856a80" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{21}{2}" :db/id 17592186058870} {:answer/id #uuid "2c81b1e5-f63c-5724-81ac-8400764b9ed8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{7}" :db/id 17592186058871}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186058870} :answer-field/id #uuid "bfde7113-aa52-5603-817f-a4c288821339" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186058866}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "8b4e7858-1264-5def-86e5-7598a8adf5a9" :question/math-academy-id "q-67329" :question/problem "Solve the equation $\frac{6}{x-3}=\frac{2}{x+6}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we note that - $x=3$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero - $x=-6$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the right-hand side zero We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows: $$ \frac{a}{b}=\frac{c}{d}\,⟹\,\frac{b}{a}=\frac{d}{c} $$ The above technique works whenever $a$ and $c$ are both different from zero. Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows: $$ \frac{x-3}{6}=\frac{x+6}{2} $$ Next, we write both fractions using the least common denominator, $6.$ The equation becomes $$ \frac{x-3}{6}=\frac{3x+18}{6}. $$ We can now solve this equation with the addition and the multiplication principles: $$ \begin{aligned}6\cdot \frac{x-3}{6} & =6\cdot \frac{3x+18}{6} \\ x-3 & =3x+18 \\ x-3x & =18+3 \\ -2x & =21 \\ \left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)(-2x) & =\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)21 \\ (-\cancel{\frac{1}{2}})(-\cancel{2}x) & =\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)21 \\ x & =-\frac{21}{2}\end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186060866 :tutorial/content "Let's now prove the sum formula for sine: $$ \sin(A+B) = \sin A\cos B + \cos A\sin B $$ To start with, we need to use the *difference* formula for *cosine*: $$ \cos(A-B) = \cos A\cos B + \sin A\sin B $$ If you haven't seen this formula yet, don't worry. You'll learn more about it, including how it's proved using the unit circle, in a separate lesson. Now, if we replace $A$ with $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - A\right)$ in the difference formula for cosine, we get $$ \cos\left(\dfrac\pi2 - A-B\right) = \cos \left(\dfrac\pi2 - A\right)\cos B + \sin\left(\dfrac\pi2 - A\right)\sin B $$ i.e. $$ \cos\left(\dfrac\pi2 - (A+B)\right) = \cos \left(\dfrac\pi2 - A\right)\cos B + \sin\left(\dfrac\pi2 - A\right)\sin B. $$ Next, using the cofunction identities $$ \begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}(\frac{\pi }{2}-(A+B)) & =\operatorname{sin}(A+B) \\ \operatorname{cos}(\frac{\pi }{2}-A) & =\operatorname{sin}A \\ \operatorname{sin}(\frac{\pi }{2}-A) & =\operatorname{cos}A\end{aligned} $$ the identity above reduces to $$ \sin(A+B) = \sin A\cos B + \cos A\sin B $$ as required." :tutorial/id #uuid "27cf015f-7be2-50f5-aed3-a5dc1f2cb26e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 13284 :tutorial/title "Proving the Sum Formula"} {:db/id 17592186060876 :tutorial/content "The Pythagorean identity is $$ \cos^2{\theta}+\sin^2{\theta}=1. $$ We can use the Pythagorean identity to simplify trigonometric expressions. For example, let's try to simplify the following: $$ 2\sin \theta \left(\sin \theta + \dfrac {\cos^2 \theta} {\sin \theta}\right) $$ We first expand the parentheses, and then simplify the resulting expression: $$ \begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}\theta (\operatorname{sin}\theta +\frac{{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta }{\operatorname{sin}\theta }) & =2{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta +2\operatorname{sin}\theta \cdot \frac{{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta }{\operatorname{sin}\theta } \\ & =2{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta +2\enclose{updiagonalstrike}{\operatorname{sin}\theta }\cdot \frac{{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta }{\enclose{updiagonalstrike}{\operatorname{sin}\theta }} \\ & =2{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta +2{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta \\ & =2({\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta +{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta )\end{aligned} $$ Now, we can use the Pythagorean identity to rewrite the expression in the parentheses, as follows: $$ 2(\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta) =2\cdot 1 = 2 $$ Therefore, we conclude that $$ 2\sin \theta \left(\sin \theta + \dfrac {\cos^2 \theta} {\sin \theta}\right) = 2. $$" :tutorial/id #uuid "feab366d-3090-5d3c-80e0-82278d6e3ea3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2403 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186060890 :tutorial/content "The following two identities are known as the **sum and difference formulas for tangent**: $$ \begin{aligned} \tan (x + y) &= \frac{\tan x + \tan y}{1 - \tan x\tan y} \\ \tan (x - y) &= \frac{\tan x - \tan y}{1 + \tan x\tan y} \end{aligned} $$ We can use the sum and difference rules to find the exact values of some trigonometric ratios. For example, let's use the sum rule to find the value of $$ \tan(75^\circ) $$ We start by writing $75^\circ$ as a sum of special angles: $$ 75^\circ = {\color{blue}45^\circ} + {\color{red}30^\circ} $$ We now apply the sum formula for tangent as follows: $$ \begin{aligned} \tan (75^{∘}) &= \tan (30^{∘} + 45^{∘}) \\ &= \frac{\tan 30^{∘} + \tan 45^{∘}}{1 - \tan 30^{∘}\tan 45^{∘}} \\ &= ((\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3} + 1))/((1 - \frac{\sqrt{3}}{3} \cdot 1)) \\ &= ((\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3} + 1))/((1 - \frac{\sqrt{3}}{3})) \end{aligned} $$ We can simplify this fraction by multiplying the numerator and denominator by $3$: $$ \begin{aligned} \tan (75^{∘}) &= ((\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3} + 1))/((1 - \frac{\sqrt{3}}{3})) \\ &= (3 \cdot (\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3} + 1))/(3 \cdot (1 - \frac{\sqrt{3}}{3})) \\ &= \frac{\sqrt{3} + 3}{3 - \sqrt{3}} \\ &= \frac{3 + \sqrt{3}}{3 - \sqrt{3}} \end{aligned} $$ Finally, we rationalize the denominator: $$ \begin{aligned} \tan (75^{∘}) &= \frac{3 + \sqrt{3}}{3 - \sqrt{3}} \\ &= \frac{3 + \sqrt{3}}{3 - \sqrt{3}} \cdot \frac{3 + \sqrt{3}}{3 + \sqrt{3}} \\ &= (3^{2} + 6\sqrt{3} + (\sqrt{3})^{2})/(3^{2} - (\sqrt{3})^{2}) \\ &= \frac{9 + 6\sqrt{3} + 3}{9 - 3} \\ &= \frac{12 + 6\sqrt{3}}{6} \\ &= 2 + \sqrt{3} \end{aligned} $$ Therefore, we conclude that $$ \tan (75^\circ) = 2+\sqrt 3 $$" :tutorial/id #uuid "367c13cc-df0b-56b3-86ab-db2e2b6d8e98" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2561 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186060894 :tutorial/content "To understand why the derivative of sine is cosine, we need to use the definition of the derivative: $$ \dfrac {\textrm{d}} {\textrm{d}x} (\sin x) = \lim_{h\rightarrow 0}\dfrac{\sin(x+h) - \sin x}{h} $$ Now, the so-called **addition formula for sine** states that $$ \sin(x+h) = \sin(x)\cos(h)+\cos (x) \sin(h). $$ By using the addition formula for sine, we can rewrite our expression for the derivative as follows: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x) & =\lim_{h\to 0}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(h)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(h)\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)}{h} \\ & =\lim_{h\to 0}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)(\operatorname{cos}⁡(h)-1)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(h)}{h} \\ & =\lim_{h\to 0}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\frac{(\operatorname{cos}⁡(h)-1)}{h}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(h)}{h}) \\ & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\underbrace{\lim_{h\to 0}\frac{(\operatorname{cos}⁡(h)-1)}{h}}_{0}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\underbrace{\lim_{h\to 0}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(h)}{h}}_{1} \\ & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\end{aligned} $$ In the last step, we used two important results for trigonometric limits: $$ \lim_{h\rightarrow 0} \dfrac{1 - \cos(h)}{h}=0 \qquad \text{and} \qquad \lim_{h\rightarrow 0} \dfrac{\sin(h)}{h}=1. $$ Deriving these results requires separate discussions, which we'll leave to future topics." :tutorial/id #uuid "8a25dc2a-846b-5554-9cc7-682b81f17e0f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2619 :tutorial/title "Justifying the Formula for the Derivative of Sine"} {:db/id 17592186060900 :tutorial/content "The following identities are called the **cofunction identities**. We can split them into three main groups. - Sine and **co**sine: $$ \begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}x & =\operatorname{cos}(\frac{\pi }{2}-x) \\ \operatorname{cos}x & =\operatorname{sin}(\frac{\pi }{2}-x)\end{aligned} $$ - Tangent and **co**tangent: $$ \begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}x & =\operatorname{cot}(\frac{\pi }{2}-x) \\ \operatorname{cot}x & =\operatorname{tan}(\frac{\pi }{2}-x)\end{aligned} $$ - Secant and **co**secant: $$ \begin{aligned}\operatorname{sec}x & =\operatorname{csc}(\frac{\pi }{2}-x) \\ \operatorname{csc}x & =\operatorname{sec}(\frac{\pi }{2}-x)\end{aligned} $$" :tutorial/id #uuid "36d44b9d-95ea-5dc0-9755-26eddfd26232" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2682 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186060947 :tutorial/content "The formula for continuously compounded growth, given by $$ P=P_0 e^{rt} $$ is actually equal to the compound interest equation $$ \begin{aligned} P &= P_0 \left(1 + \dfrac r n \right)^{nt}, \end{aligned} $$ for extremely large $n$ (in other words, as $n \rightarrow \infty$). To demonstrate, let's take the case of $P_0=1$, $r=1$, and $t=1$. Then the formula for continuously compounded growth gives $$ \begin{aligned} P &= P_{0}e^{1 \cdot 1} \\ &= 1e^{1 \cdot 1} \\ &= e \\ &= 2.7182818… \end{aligned} $$ and the compound interest equation is $$ \begin{aligned} P &= P_{0}(1 + \frac{r}{n})^{nt} \\ &= 1(1 + \frac{1}{n})^{n \cdot 1} \\ &= (1 + \frac{1}{n})^{n} \end{aligned} $$ If we substitute a large value of $n$, say $$ n=1\,000\,000 $$ then we get $$ \begin{aligned} P &= (1 + \frac{1}{1000000})^{1000000} \\ &= (1.000001)^{1000000} \\ &\approx 2.718280 \\ &\approx e \end{aligned} $$ This result matches up nicely with our result from the formula for continuously compounded growth! Here, we demonstrated that the result holds for the special case where $P_0=r=t=1$. However, it is possible to show that the formula is always true." :tutorial/id #uuid "9199edc0-173e-5919-a918-157af0b90048" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3408 :tutorial/title "The Relationship Between Continuous Compounding and the Compound Interest Equation"} {:db/id 17592186060957 :tutorial/content "We've practiced using the sum and difference formulas for tangent. But where do they come from? To derive the sum formula for tangent, we start off by recalling the sum and difference formulas for sine and cosine: $$ \begin{aligned} \sin (x + y) &= \sin x\cos y + \cos x\sin y \\ \cos (x + y) &= \cos x\cos y - \sin x\sin y \end{aligned} $$ Now, using the identity $$ \tan\theta = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} $$ we can divide $\sin(x+ y)$ by $\cos(x+ y)$ to get $\tan(x+ y)$. Dividing, we have $$ \dfrac{\sin(x+ y)}{\cos(x+ y)} = \dfrac{\sin x\cos y + \cos x\sin y}{\cos x\cos y - \sin x\sin y} $$ and simplifying, we reach $$ \tan(x+y) = \dfrac{\sin x\cos y + \cos x\sin y}{\cos x\cos y - \sin x\sin y} $$ To write the right-hand side in terms of tangent only, we divide the numerator and denominator by $\cos x\cos y$. This gives $$ {\begin{array}{rl}\displaystyle \tan ( x + y ) & \displaystyle = {\displaystyle \frac{\sin x \cos y + \cos x \sin y}{\cos x \cos y - \sin x \sin y}} \\ \displaystyle & \displaystyle = {\displaystyle \frac{( {\displaystyle \frac{\sin x \cos y}{\cos x \cos y}} + {\displaystyle \frac{\cos x \sin y}{\cos x \cos y}} )}{( {\displaystyle \frac{\cos x \cos y}{\cos x \cos y}} - {\displaystyle \frac{\sin x \sin y}{\cos x \cos y}} )}} \\ \displaystyle & \displaystyle = {\displaystyle \frac{( {\displaystyle \frac{\sin x \cancel{\cos y}}{\cos x \cancel{\cos y}}} + {\displaystyle \frac{\cancel{\cos x} \sin y}{\cancel{\cos x} \cos y}} )}{( 1 - {\displaystyle \frac{\sin x \sin y}{\cos x \cos y}} )}} \\ \displaystyle & \displaystyle = {\displaystyle \frac{( {\displaystyle \frac{\sin x}{\cos x}} + {\displaystyle \frac{\sin y}{\cos y}} )}{( 1 - {\displaystyle \frac{\sin x}{\cos x}} \cdot {\displaystyle \frac{\sin y}{\cos y}} )}} \\ \displaystyle & \displaystyle = {\displaystyle \frac{\tan x + \tan y}{1 - \tan x \tan y}} .\end{array}} $$ We can derive the difference formula for tangent in a similar way." :tutorial/id #uuid "ea32c1b4-9316-5da5-9075-239dcda6e2ee" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4146 :tutorial/title "Deriving the Sum and Difference Formulas for Tangent"} {:answer/id #uuid "a175a8cb-a6ee-5116-a42e-7718588e0c8a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2^{x}}{\ln 2}(\frac{1}{x} - So, if we attempt to evaluate the limit directly, we get $$ \lim_{x \to 0}\dfrac{\sec x -1}{x} = \dfrac{\sec 0-1}{0} = \dfrac 00 $$ which is an indeterminate form. Instead, let's recall the following special limit: $$ \lim_{x \to 0} \dfrac{1-\cos x}{x} = 0 $$ Now, multiplying both the numerator and denominator by $\cos x$, we can rewrite the expression and evaluate the limit: $$ \begin{aligned} \lim_{x \to 0}\frac{\sec x - 1}{x} &= \lim_{x \to 0}((\sec x - 1)\cos x)/(x\cos x) \\ &= \lim_{x \to 0}((\frac{1}{\cos x} - 1)\cos x)/(x\cos x) \\ &= \lim_{x \to 0}\frac{1 - \cos x}{x\cos x} \\ &= \lim_{x \to 0}\frac{1 - \cos x}{x} \cdot lim_(x → 0)\frac{1}{\cos x} \\ &= 0 \cdot (1)/(\cos (0)) \\ &= 0 \cdot 1 \\ &= 0 \end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186063914 :question/id #uuid "65a0be54-6801-5337-b68f-01c7049365cb" :question/math-academy-id "e-10088" :question/problem "

Let $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_{185}$ be a random sample of size $n = 185$ from a population with the probability mass function given above. Find an approximation in terms of $\Phi(z)$ for $P(|\overline{X}| \gt 0.1).$ *Note: $\Phi(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.*" :question/worked-solution "Suppose that $X_1, X_2,\ldots, X_n$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a population with population mean $\mu$ and population standard deviation $\sigma.$ The central limit theorem (or CLT) states that for sufficiently large $n,$ the distribution of the sample mean $\overline{X}$ can be approximated as $$ \overline{X}\sim N\!\left(\mu,\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right). $$ In our case: - the sample size is $$ n = 185, $$ - the population mean is $$ \begin{aligned}\mu & =\text{E}[X] \\ & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}f({x}_{i}) \\ & =-3\cdot 0.4+(-1)\cdot 0.1+1\cdot 0.1+3\cdot 0.4 \\ & =-1.2-0.1+0.1+1.2 \\ & =0,\end{aligned} $$ - the population variance is $$ \begin{aligned}{\sigma }^{2} & =\text{Var}[X] \\ & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\ & =((-3)^{2}\cdot 0.4+(-1)^{2}\cdot 0.1+{1}^{2}\cdot 0.1+{3}^{2}\cdot 0.4)-{0}^{2} \\ & =(3.6+0.1+0.1+3.6)-0 \\ & =7.4.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, by the CLT, we have that the distribution of the sample mean can be approximated as $$ \begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}) \\ & ∼N\,(0,\frac{7.4}{185}) \\ & ∼N(0,0.04).\end{aligned} $$ We want to find $P(|\overline{X}| \gt 0.1).$ So, we convert $\overline{X}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring: $$ \begin{aligned}P(|\overset{―}{X}|>0.1) & =P(\overset{―}{X}<-0.1)+P(\overset{―}{X}>0.1) \\ & ≈P(Z<\frac{-0.1-0}{\sqrt{0.04}})+P(Z>\frac{0.1-0}{\sqrt{0.04}}) \\ & =P(Z<-0.5)+P(Z>0.5) \\ & =P(Z<-0.5)+1-P(Z<0.5) \\ & =1+Φ(-0.5)-Φ(0.5).\end{aligned} $$ By the symmetry of the normal distribution, we have $$ \qquad \Phi(-0.5) = 1-\Phi(0.5). $$ Therefore, we conclude that $$ \begin{aligned}P(|\overset{―}{X}|>0.1) & =1+Φ(-0.5)-Φ(0.5) \\ & =1+(1-Φ(0.5))-Φ(0.5) \\ & =2-2Φ(0.5) \\ & =2(1-Φ(0.5)).\end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186063915 :question/id #uuid "a31b1e5c-c4e3-57df-9e05-5f2fdc6b3397" :question/math-academy-id "e-10090" :question/problem "Let $X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_{100}$ be a random sample of size $n=100$ from a population with probability density function $$ f(x) = {\left\{ \begin{array}{ll}{\displaystyle \frac{2}{9}} x , & 0 \le x \le 3 , \\ 0 , & \text{otherwise} .\end{array} \right. } $$ Given that the population variance $\sigma^2 = 0.5,$ calculate $P( \overline{X}>1.9 ).$ *Hint: A table of values of $\Phi(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $\Phi(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.*
$z$$\, 0.01 \,$$\, 0.02 \,$$\, 0.03 \,$
$\, -1.5 \,$$\, 0.0655 \,$$\, 0.0643 \,$$\, 0.0630 \,$
$\, -1.4 \,$$\, 0.0793 \,$$\, 0.0778 \,$$\, 0.0764 \,$
$\, -1.3 \,$$\, 0.0951 \,$$\, 0.0934 \,$$\, 0.0918 \,$
" :question/worked-solution "Suppose that $X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_n$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a population with population mean $\mu$ and population standard deviation $\sigma.$ The central limit theorem (or CLT) states that for sufficiently large $n,$ the distribution of the sample mean $\overline{X}$ can be approximated as $$ \overline{X}\sim N\!\left(\mu,\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right). $$ In our case: - the sample size is $$ \begin{aligned}n & =100,\end{aligned} $$ - the population mean is $$ \begin{aligned}\mu & =\text{E}[X] \\ & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{3}x\cdot \frac{2}{9}x\,\text{d}x \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{2}{9}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\ & ={[\frac{2{x}^{3}}{27}]}_{0}^{3} \\ & =2,\end{aligned} $$ - the population variance is $\sigma^2 = 0.5.$ Therefore, by the CLT, we have that the distribution of the sample mean can be approximated as $$ \begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}) \\ & ∼N\,(2,\frac{0.5}{100}) \\ & ∼N(2,0.005).\end{aligned} $$ We want to find $P( \overline{X}>1.9 ).$ So, we convert $\overline{X}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring: $$ \begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}>1.9) & =P(Z>\frac{1.9-2}{\sqrt{0.005}}) \\ & ≈P(Z>-1.41).\end{aligned} $$ Using the symmetry of the normal distribution, we have $$ \begin{aligned}P(Z>-1.41) & =1-P(Z\le -1.41) \\ & =1-Φ(-1.41).\end{aligned} $$ From the table, we have that $$ \Phi(-1.41) = 0.0793. $$ Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}>1.9) & =1-Φ(-1.41) \\ & =1-0.0793 \\ & =0.9207.\end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186063962 :question/id #uuid "2fb03f0f-25c2-57a6-9e33-da837af2f339" :question/math-academy-id "e-1329" :question/problem "Factor the expression $y^2 + \dfrac{2}{5}y + \dfrac{1}{25}.$" :question/worked-solution "The "square of a sum" formula states that $$ x^2 + {\color{red}{2}}{\color{blue}{a}} x + a^2 = (x+{\color{blue}{a}})^2 . $$ We will use this formula to factor the given trinomial. Our trinomial is $$ y^2 + \dfrac{2}{5}y + \dfrac{1}{25}. $$ First, we write the constant term as a perfect square: $$ \begin{aligned}{y}^{2}+\frac{2}{5}y+{\left(\frac{1}{5}\right)}^{2} & \end{aligned} $$ Then, we factor a $2$ out of the linear term: $$ \begin{aligned}{y}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{1}{5}y+{\left(\frac{1}{5}\right)}^{2}\end{aligned} $$ Finally, we factor the trinomial using the square of sum formula with ${\color{blue}{a}} = {\color{blue}{\dfrac 1 5}}.$ This gives $$ \begin{aligned}{(y+\frac{1}{5})}^{2}.\end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186063980 :question/id #uuid "9c9b5972-f775-5cbe-8e66-2a0309f24f0e" :question/math-academy-id "e-142" :question/problem "Find the slope of the tangent to the curve $y = x^2 + \dfrac {1}{x}$ at the point where $x=2.$" :question/worked-solution "Let $f(x)=x^2+\dfrac 1 x.$ The slope of the tangent at $x=2$ is equal to $f'(2).$ Computing the derivative, we get $$ \begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{x}) \\ & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}+{x}^{-1}) \\ & =2\cdot x-{x}^{-2} \\ & =2x-{x}^{-2}.\end{aligned} $$ Now, we evaluate at $x=2$ and get $$ \begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(2) & =2(2)-(2{)}^{-2} \\ & =4-\frac{1}{4} \\ & =\frac{15}{4}.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the slope of the tangent to the curve is $\dfrac{15}{4}.$"} {:db/id 17592186063986 :question/id #uuid "0317d27d-9501-5de5-a55a-b9a73ce39500" :question/math-academy-id "e-14306" :question/problem "Simplify $-6x^2\left(\dfrac{x^3}{2}+3x^2\right).$" :question/worked-solution "We multiply each term inside the parentheses by the term outside the parentheses, simplify using the rules of exponents, and then we add the results together: $$ \begin{aligned}-6{x}^{2}(\frac{{x}^{3}}{2}+3{x}^{2}) &= (-6{x}^{2})\left(\frac{{x}^{3}}{2}\right)+(-6{x}^{2})(3{x}^{2}) \\ &= (-6{x}^{2})(\frac{1}{2}{x}^{3})+(-6{x}^{2})(3{x}^{2}) \\ &= ((-6)\cdot \frac{1}{2})({x}^{3}\cdot {x}^{2})+((-6)\cdot 3)({x}^{2}\cdot {x}^{2}) \\ &= (-3)({x}^{3+2})+(-18)({x}^{2+2}) \\ &= -3{x}^{5}-18{x}^{4}\end{aligned} $$ **Note:** We provide the answer in *standard form*, with the terms arranged by degree in descending order."} {:db/id 17592186064025 :question/id #uuid "87c5af76-7652-525a-aeb2-d419bab613e0" :question/math-academy-id "e-227" :question/problem "Air is leaking from a spherical balloon at the rate of $500\pi\,\text{cm}^3/\text{s}.$ How fast is the radius of the balloon decreasing when the radius is $10\,\text{cm}?$ ![](images/46/460fd4059be2c655e01b89db2738225a50578b5c76bbe048f83312f0bff655ec.png)" :question/worked-solution "Let $r$ be the radius of the balloon and $V$ its volume. Both $r$ and $V$ change with time. In particular, we are given $$ \dfrac{\textrm dV}{\textrm dt} = -500\pi\,\text{cm}^3/\text{s}, $$ and we want to find $\dfrac{\textrm dr}{\textrm dt}$ when $r=10\,\text{cm}.$ To start, let's write down the volume formula for the sphere and then differentiate it using implicit differentiation. We get $$ \begin{aligned}V & =\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(V) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}r}(\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 4\pi {r}^{2}.\end{aligned} $$ Now we can substitute the given information $\dfrac{\textrm dV}{\textrm dt} = -500\pi$ and $r=10,$ and solve for $\dfrac{\textrm dr}{\textrm dt}.$ We get $$ \begin{aligned}-500\pi & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 4\pi (10)^{2} \\ -500\pi & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 400\pi \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{5}{4} \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =-1.25.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the radius of the balloon is decreasing at a rate of $1.25\,\text{cm}/\text{s}$ when the radius is $10\,\text{cm}.$"} {:db/id 17592186064028 :question/id #uuid "69ba4325-7189-590d-95dd-b11487b632c8" :question/math-academy-id "e-230" :question/problem "An $8\,\text{m}$ tall lamppost is casting a shadow of a $2\,\text{m}$ man onto the ground. The man walks away from the lamppost with a speed of $2.4\,\text{m/s}.$ How fast is the length of the man's shadow changing?" :question/worked-solution "Let's draw a figure according to the given data. ![](images/29/29ef832326fff9e5b274c92ae51f2f32a88d463980fd4c109773086c344a76bb.png) In the figure, $x$ is the man's distance from the lamp, while $y$ is the length of his shadow. Both $x$ and $y$ change with time. In particular, we know that the man's velocity is $$ \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} = 2.4\,\textrm{m/s}. $$ Notice that the man's velocity is *positive* because he is walking away from the lamp, and therefore, the distance between him and the lamp *increases* with time. Since we want to calculate $\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t},$ we need to find a relation between $x$ and $y.$ Since the two triangles are similar, the ratios between the corresponding sides are equal, and we have $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{x+y}{8} & =\frac{y}{2} \\ 2x+2y & =8y \\ 2x & =6y \\ y & =\frac{1}{3}x.\end{aligned} $$ We differentiate both sides of the above equation with respect to $t$ using the chain rule, and we get $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{3}x) \\ & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned} $$ Finally, substituting $\dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} =2.4\,\textrm{m/s}$ into the above gives $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot (2.4) \\ & =\frac{2.4}{3} \\ & =0.8\,\text{m/s}.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the length of the man's shadow increases at a rate of $0.8\,\textrm{m/s}.$"} {:db/id 17592186064029 :question/id #uuid "a669adb9-c12e-520d-994b-cddf4f9fedb6" :question/math-academy-id "e-233" :question/problem "Maria is flying a kite $K$ at an angle of $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ to the horizontal. The kite's shadow $S$ is projected onto the ground vertically below the kite. If the kite is moving towards Maria with a speed of $5\,\text{ft}/\text{s},$ what is the speed of the kite's shadow? *Hint*: Remember that speed is always positive or zero. ![](images/1a/1a00ce10db2d8a0fa292bd3ca67744e7cbaafcf1861cbbdc049832d287926d28.png)" :question/worked-solution "![](images/69/69402f16f81a6653e1fdd313c314ac72db7f5514501af1ac147b5e499b305233.png) Let $x$ be the distance between María and the shadow, and let $z$ be the distance between Maria and the kite. We want to find $\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm dt}.$ To do this, let's start by setting up a relation between $x$ and $z.$ Relative to the angle $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{3},$ the sides $x$ and $z$ are the adjacent and hypotenuse, respectively. So, we have $$ \begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right) & =\frac{x}{z} \\ \frac{1}{2} & =\frac{x}{z} \\ x & =\frac{1}{2}z.\end{aligned} $$ Now, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, and we get $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{2}z) \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{1}{2}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned} $$ We know that $\dfrac{\textrm d z}{\textrm dt} = -5\,\textrm{ft/s}$ (negative because the distance between Maria and the kite is decreasing). Substituting this into the above gives $$ \dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm dt} = \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot (-5) = -2.5. $$ Therefore, the speed of the shadow is $2.5\,\textrm{ft/s}.$"} {:db/id 17592186064030 :question/id #uuid "7c740ffe-3391-52cc-b8fd-7fb9a54e58cf" :question/math-academy-id "e-234" :question/problem "Yurii is flying a kite $K$ with a string of length $45\,\textrm{m}.$ The angle of elevation of the kite $\theta$ decreases at a rate of $\dfrac{\pi}{15}$ radians per second. At what rate is the altitude of the kite is decreasing at the moment when $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{6}?$ ![](images/83/83f63ada35f2d9f64cd4b5013ccfcc86a97e48c7d19b49c403d21222a2e14d7b.png)" :question/worked-solution "![](images/04/04784c267488ef2073c526aed683e86ca0a00d00af64eb994ce596c0cce629d9.png) In the figure, $y$ is the altitude of the kite, and $z$ is the distance between the kite and Yurii. The quantity $z=45$ meters does not change with time because the kite string's length is fixed. We wish to calculate $\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}.$ To do this, let's start by setting up a relation between $y$ and $z.$ Relative to the angle $\theta,$ the sides $y$ and $z$ are the opposite and hypotenuse, respectively. So, we have $$ \begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta & =\frac{y}{z} \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta & =\frac{y}{45} \\ y & =45\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned} $$ Now, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, and we get $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(45\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =(45\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned} $$ From the given information, we have $$ \displaystyle \dfrac{\textrm d \theta}{\textrm d t} = -\dfrac{\pi}{15} $$ (negative because the angle is decreasing) and $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{6}.$ Substituting these values into the above, we reach $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =(45\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right))\left(-\frac{\pi }{15}\right) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =45\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)\left(-\frac{\pi }{15}\right) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{3\pi \sqrt{3}}{2}.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the rate that the kite is losing altitude is $\dfrac{3\pi\sqrt3}{2} \,\text{m/s}.$"} {:db/id 17592186064032 :question/id #uuid "6ce9d38b-08d9-5372-b501-298970a2f11f" :question/math-academy-id "e-236" :question/problem "A conical flask has a height of $20\,\text{cm}.$ The radius at the bottom of the flask is $10\,\text{cm}.$ The flask has a very narrow opening at the top, and a chemist is pouring a chemical into the flask. If the level (i.e., height) of the chemical in the flask is increasing at a rate of $2\,\text{cm/min}$, find the rate at which volume of the chemical is increasing when the chemical level is $4\,\text{cm}.$ ![](images/eb/eb454cec7cd4c38997ee5c8e9e29fed87f491f5f47066271613bb51e0aae5363.png)" :question/worked-solution "First, let's consider the dimensions of the flask. We call $H=20\,\text{cm}$ the height of the conical flask, and $R=10\,\text{cm}$ its radius at the bottom. These quantities are fixed and do not change with time. Now, let's consider the chemical level. We call $h$ the distance from the top of the flask to the surface of the chemical, $r$ the radius of the flask at the chemical surface, and $v$ the volume of the empty space in the flask. All of these quantities change with time. In particular, we are given that $$ \dfrac{\textrm dh}{\textrm dt} = -2\,\text{cm}/\text{min}, $$ which is negative because the distance from the top of the flask to the chemical surface decreases as the chemist pours the chemical into the flask. We want to find the rate at which the volume being poured into the flask is changing when the chemical level is $4\,\text{cm}.$ So, we wish to find $\dfrac{\textrm dv}{\textrm dt}$ when the level of the chemical is $4\,\text{cm}.$ At this moment, we have $$ \begin{aligned}h & =H-4 \\ & =20-4 \\ & =16\,\text{cm}.\end{aligned} $$ We need to find a relation between $v$ and the variable for which we know the rate of change, which is $h.$ This is given by the formula for the volume of a cone: $$ v = \dfrac13 \pi r^2 h $$ Before we differentiate the equation with respect to time, note that $r$ also appears in the formula. So, we need to simplify the formula by writing $r$ in terms of $h.$ Note that the cones formed by the tank and the chemical must be similar. Therefore, we have $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{r}{h} & =\frac{R}{H} \\ \frac{r}{h} & =\frac{10}{20} \\ r & =\frac{h}{2}.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, we can write the volume formula as $$ \begin{aligned}v & =\frac{1}{3}\pi {\left(\frac{h}{2}\right)}^{2}h \\ v & =\frac{1}{12}\pi {h}^{3}.\end{aligned} $$ Now that we have an equation relating $v$ and $h,$ we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}v & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{12}\pi {h}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{1}{4}\pi {h}^{2}\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\end{aligned} $$ Finally, substituting the known values, we get $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{1}{4}\pi {(16)}^{2}(-2) \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} & =-128\pi \,{\text{cm}}^{3}/\text{min}.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the volume of chemical is increasing at a rate of $128\pi \, \text{cm}^3/\text{min}.$"} {:db/id 17592186064038 :question/id #uuid "368cbbae-4eff-5eff-a8f3-d3e8359447a9" :question/math-academy-id "e-364" :question/problem "Calculate $$ \displaystyle \int x^2 \,\textrm d x. $$" :question/worked-solution "We apply the power rule with $n=2$, and we get $$ \int x^2 \,\textrm d x = \dfrac{x^{2+1}}{2+1} + C = \dfrac{x^3}{3}+C. $$ Let's check by differentiating: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+C) &= \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\left(\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}\right)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) \\ &= \frac{1}{3}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3})+0 \\ &= \frac{1}{3}\cdot 3{x}^{2} \\ &= {x}^{2}\,✓\end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186064039 :question/id #uuid "818f4fbe-e251-57bd-90ae-b6517c6f2f89" :question/math-academy-id "e-367" :question/problem "Find the antiderivative of $\sqrt x.$" :question/worked-solution "We start by writing the square root as a rational power, $\sqrt x= x^{1/2}.$ So, we can apply the power rule with $n=\dfrac{1}{2}$ and get $$ \begin{aligned}\int \sqrt{x}\,\text{d}x & =\int {x}^{1/2}\,\text{d}x \\ & =\frac{{x}^{1/2+1}}{(\frac{1}{2}+1)}+C \\ & =\frac{{x}^{3/2}}{\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)}+C \\ & =\frac{2{x}^{3/2}}{3}+C.\end{aligned} $$ Again, let's check by differentiating: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{2{x}^{3/2}}{3}+C) &= \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\left(\frac{2{x}^{3/2}}{3}\right)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) \\ &= \frac{2}{3}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3/2})+0 \\ &= \frac{2}{3}\cdot \frac{3}{2}{x}^{3/2-1} \\ &= {x}^{1/2}\,✓\end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186064058 :question/id #uuid "6ff9c057-e61a-5648-9a49-72a70f3127bc" :question/math-academy-id "e-388" :question/problem "Evaluate the integral $$ \displaystyle \int \dfrac {x^2+2}{x^2 + 1}\, \textrm{d}x. $$" :question/worked-solution "This integral doesn't look like one of the basic ones. However, we can manipulate the numerator a bit to make it look more like the denominator, which reveals a more familiar expression: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}+2}{{x}^{2}+1} & =\frac{{x}^{2}+1+1}{{x}^{2}+1} \\ & =\frac{{x}^{2}+1}{{x}^{2}+1}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1} \\ & =1+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}.\end{aligned} $$ Remembering that $$ \int \dfrac{1}{x^2+1} \textrm dx = \arctan(x), $$ we can now calculate the integral and get $$ \begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{x}^{2}+2}{{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x & =\int (1+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1})\text{d}x \\ & =\int 1\,\text{d}x+\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x \\ & =x+\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x)+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186064059 :question/id #uuid "81e3df9e-e5ab-57ec-9a82-149a277e94f0" :question/math-academy-id "e-3890" :question/problem "If $f'(x) = \dfrac{5}{|x|\sqrt{x^2 - 1}} - 2x,$ then $f(x)=$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that $$ \int \dfrac{1}{|x|\sqrt{x^2 - 1}} \, \textrm dx = \operatorname{arcsec} \, x. $$ Then we have $$ \begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\int {f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x \\ & =\int (\frac{5}{|x|\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}}-2x)\text{d}x \\ & =\int \frac{5}{|x|\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x-\int 2x\,\text{d}x \\ & =5\int \frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x-2\int x\,\text{d}x \\ & =5\operatorname{arcsec} \,(x)-2\cdot \frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+C \\ & =5\operatorname{arcsec} \,(x)-{x}^{2}+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186064069 :question/id #uuid "e0bb9783-9d30-5139-a2c0-aae55ea18733" :question/math-academy-id "e-410" :question/problem "Evaluate $$ \displaystyle \int _{1}^2\dfrac 1 {x^3}\, \textrm d x. $$" :question/worked-solution "Taking the antiderivative and evaluating the difference at the bounds, we get $$ \begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{x}^{-3}\,\text{d}x \\ & =\frac{{x}^{-3+1}}{-3+1}{|}_{1}^{2} \\ & =-\frac{{x}^{-2}}{2}{|}_{1}^{2} \\ & =-\frac{1}{2}({2}^{-2}-{1}^{-2}) \\ & =-\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{4}-1) \\ & =-\frac{1}{2}\left(-\frac{3}{4}\right) \\ & =\frac{3}{8}.\end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186064071 :question/id #uuid "eff323d1-4e70-5490-8e41-9fbf00c387f5" :question/math-academy-id "e-446" :question/problem "Calculate $$ \displaystyle\int (3x+1)^3 \, \textrm{d}x . $$" :question/worked-solution "Let $u=3x+1.$ Then differentiating with respect to $x$ gives $$ \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = 3\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm d x = \dfrac 1 3 \textrm d u. $$ We now write our integral in terms of $u,$ calculate the integral as normal, and write the final answer in terms of $x$ at the very end: $$ \begin{aligned}\int (3x+1)^{3}\,\text{d}x & =\int {u}^{3}\cdot \frac{1}{3}\text{d}u \\ & =\frac{1}{3}\int {u}^{3}\text{d}u \\ & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot \frac{{u}^{4}}{4}+C \\ & =\frac{1}{12}{u}^{4}+C \\ & =\frac{1}{12}(3x+1)^{4}+C\end{aligned} $$ Let's double-check that our result is correct. If we differentiate the result, then it should come out to the original integrand: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[\frac{1}{12}(3x+1)^{4}+C] & =\frac{1}{12}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[(3x+1)^{4}]+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) \\ & =\frac{1}{12}\cdot 4(3x+1)^{3}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3x+1)+0 \\ & =\frac{1}{3}(3x+1)^{3}\cdot 3 \\ & =(3x+1)^{3}\,✓\end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186064072 :question/id #uuid "e469c042-9619-55d4-b745-d4ed26251d80" :question/math-academy-id "e-447" :question/problem "Calculate $$ \displaystyle\int \dfrac{2}{(1-x)^3} \, \textrm{d}x . $$" :question/worked-solution "First, we rewrite the integral as $$ \displaystyle\int 2(1-x)^{-3} \, \textrm{d}x . $$ Let $u=1-x.$ Then differentiating with respect to $x$ gives $$ \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = -1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm d x = -\textrm d u. $$ We now write our integral in terms of $u,$ calculate the integral as normal, and write the final answer in terms of $x$ at the very end: $$ \begin{aligned}\int 2(1-x)^{-3}\,\text{d}x & =\int 2{u}^{-3}\cdot (-1)\text{d}u \\ & =-2\int {u}^{-3}\text{d}u \\ & =-2\cdot \frac{{u}^{-2}}{-2}+C \\ & ={u}^{-2}+C \\ & =(1-x)^{-2}+C \\ & =\frac{1}{(1-x)^{2}}+C.\end{aligned} $$ Let's double-check that our result is correct. If we differentiate the result, then it should come out to the original integrand: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[\frac{1}{(1-x)^{2}}+C] & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[\frac{1}{(1-x)^{2}}]+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) \\ & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[(1-x)^{-2}]+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) \\ & =-2(1-x)^{-3}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(1-x)+0 \\ & =-\frac{2}{(1-x)^{3}}\cdot (-1) \\ & =\frac{2}{(1-x)^{3}}\,✓\end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186064075 :question/id #uuid "e416cb5c-22df-55e4-a3cb-c6b5dfc650c3" :question/math-academy-id "e-448" :question/problem "Calculate $$ \displaystyle\int\sqrt{1-5x}\,\textrm d x. $$" :question/worked-solution "First, we rewrite the integral as $$ \displaystyle\int(1-5x)^{1/2}\,\textrm d x. $$ Now, we let $u=1-5x.$ Then differentiating with respect to $x$ gives $$ \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = -5\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm d x = -\dfrac 1 5 \textrm d u. $$ We now write our integral in terms of $u,$ calculate the integral as normal, and write the final answer in terms of $x$ at the very end: $$ \begin{aligned}\int (1-5x)^{1/2}\,\text{d}x & =\int {u}^{1/2}\cdot \left(-\frac{1}{5}\right)\,\text{d}u \\ & =-\frac{1}{5}\int {u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\ & =-\frac{1}{5}\cdot \frac{2}{3}{u}^{3/2}+C \\ & =-\frac{2}{15}{u}^{3/2}+C \\ & =-\frac{2}{15}(1-5x)^{3/2}+C \\ & =-\frac{2}{15}\sqrt{(1-5x)^{3}}+C\end{aligned} $$ Let's double-check that our result is correct. If we differentiate the result, then it should come out to the original integrand: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[-\frac{2}{15}\sqrt{(1-5x)^{3}}+C] & =-\frac{2}{15}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[\sqrt{(1-5x)^{3}}]+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) \\ & =-\frac{2}{15}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[(1-5x)^{3/2}]+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) \\ & =-\frac{2}{15}\cdot \frac{3}{2}(1-5x)^{1/2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(1-5x)+0 \\ & =-\frac{1}{5}(1-5x)^{1/2}\cdot (-5) \\ & =(1-5x)^{1/2}\,✓\end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186064079 :question/id #uuid "2c4912bd-290a-5074-b11b-459c77b7e238" :question/math-academy-id "e-451" :question/problem "Calculate $$ \displaystyle \int\left(\dfrac{1}{1+2x} + \dfrac{1}{1-2x}\right)\,\textrm d x. $$" :question/worked-solution "Let's solve this using the general formula: $$ \begin{aligned}\int (\frac{1}{1+2x}+\frac{1}{1-2x})\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{1+2x}\,\text{d}x+\int \frac{1}{1-2x}\,\text{d}x \\ & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|1+2x|-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|1-2x|+C \\ & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|\frac{1+2x}{1-2x}|+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡K \\ & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(K|\frac{1+2x}{1-2x}|)\end{aligned} $$ Notice that we used the laws of logarithms to write the result as a single logarithm."} {:db/id 17592186064080 :question/id #uuid "109a6d6e-8e62-5eac-bfa8-7c059399efe8" :question/math-academy-id "e-457" :question/problem "Evaluate $$ \displaystyle \int_0^{1/2}x(1-2x)^5\,\textrm d x. $$" :question/worked-solution "Let $u=1-2x.$ Then, we have $$ \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = -2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad -\dfrac 1 2 \,\textrm d u = \textrm d x. $$ We also note that $x = \dfrac 1 2 (1-u).$ Computing our limits of integration, we get | **$x$** | $0$ | $1/2$ | | --- | --- | --- | | **$u$** | $1$ | $0$ | We can now solve the integral using our new variable $u,$ remembering to use the new limits of integration: $$ \begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1/2}x(1-2x)^{5}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{1}^{0}\frac{1}{2}\cdot (1-u)\cdot {u}^{5}\cdot \left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)\,\text{d}u \\ & =-\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{1}^{0}(1-u)\cdot {u}^{5}\,\text{d}u \\ & =-\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{1}^{0}({u}^{5}-{u}^{6})\,\text{d}u \\ & =-\frac{1}{4}{(\frac{1}{6}{u}^{6}-\frac{1}{7}{u}^{7})|}_{1}^{0} \\ & =-\frac{1}{4}([0-0]-[\frac{1}{6}-\frac{1}{7}]) \\ & =-\frac{1}{4}\left(-\frac{1}{42}\right) \\ & =\frac{1}{168}\end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186064081 :question/id #uuid "a40f6e7e-f4d3-5f3e-bf9d-99c640e36274" :question/math-academy-id "e-458" :question/problem "Calculate $$ \displaystyle \int x^3\sqrt{x^2 + 1}\, \textrm{d}x. $$" :question/worked-solution "Let $u = x^2+1.$ Then, we have $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2x\,⟹\,\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u=x\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned} $$ We can now solve the integral in terms of $u,$ and then express our final answer in terms of $x\mathbin{:}$ $$ \begin{aligned}\int {x}^{3}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x & =\int {x}^{2}\cdot x\sqrt{{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x \\ & =\int {x}^{2}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+1}\,\cdot x\,\text{d}x \\ & =\int \overbrace{{x}^{2}}^{u-1}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+1}\cdot \overbrace{x\,\text{d}x}^{\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u} \\ & =\int (u-1)\sqrt{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\ & =\frac{1}{2}\int (u-1){u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\ & =\frac{1}{2}\int ({u}^{3/2}-{u}^{1/2})\,\text{d}u \\ & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{2}{5}{u}^{5/2}-\frac{2}{3}{u}^{3/2})+C \\ & =\frac{1}{5}({x}^{2}+1)^{5/2}-\frac{1}{3}({x}^{2}+1)^{3/2}+C \\ & =\frac{1}{5}\sqrt{({x}^{2}+1)^{5}}-\frac{1}{3}\sqrt{({x}^{2}+1)^{3}}+C\end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186064092 :question/id #uuid "cb771ff3-b5a9-5900-913f-df23957760b1" :question/math-academy-id "e-472" :question/problem "Evaluate the integral $$ \displaystyle{\int_{0}^{\sqrt 2} \dfrac{1}{2+x^2}\, \textrm{d}x}. $$" :question/worked-solution "First, we rewrite the integral as $$ \begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}\frac{1}{2+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}\frac{1}{2(1+{x}^{2}/2)}\,\text{d}x \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}\frac{1}{2(1+(x/\sqrt{2})^{2})}\,\text{d}x \\ & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}\frac{1}{1+(x/\sqrt{2})^{2}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned} $$ We see that this integral now resembles the basic integral for the inverse tangent, $$ \int\dfrac{1}{1+u^2}\,\textrm d u = \arctan{u} + C. $$ We make the substitution $u=\dfrac{x}{\sqrt 2}.$ Differentiating, we get $$ \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt 2}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \sqrt 2 \,\textrm d u = \textrm d x. $$ Before substituting, we use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$
$x$ $0$ $\sqrt2$
$u$ $0$ $1$
Using the above, we can now write the integral in terms of $u,$ and evaluate: $$ \begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}\frac{1}{2+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\,\cdot \sqrt{2}\,\text{d}u \\ & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\ & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}{\operatorname{arctan}⁡u|}_{0}^{1} \\ & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡1-\operatorname{arctan}⁡0) \\ & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(\frac{\pi }{4}-0) \\ & =\frac{\pi \sqrt{2}}{8}\end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186064093 :question/id #uuid "15473603-5bb5-5a20-8fc9-e4d7589ccb38" :question/math-academy-id "e-473" :question/problem "Calculate $$ \displaystyle \int \dfrac{1}{\sin x}\left(\cot x + \sin^2 x\right)\,\textrm d x. $$" :question/worked-solution "We multiply out the parentheses and then use the identity $\dfrac{1}{\sin x } = \csc x,$ as follows: $$ \begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}(\operatorname{cot}⁡x+{\sin }^{2}⁡x)\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\cdot \operatorname{cot}⁡x+\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\cdot {\sin }^{2}⁡x)\,\text{d}x \\ & =\int (\operatorname{csc}⁡x\cdot \operatorname{cot}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\,\text{d}x \\ & =\int \operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{cot}⁡x\,\text{d}x+\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ & =-\operatorname{csc}⁡x-\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C\end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186064096 :question/id #uuid "4d4edfc8-e178-58b4-b827-e4310ead130e" :question/math-academy-id "e-485" :question/problem "Calculate $$ \displaystyle\int_0^1 \dfrac{4x-1}{x+1}\,\textrm d x. $$" :question/worked-solution "The denominator of the integrand doesn't divide the numerator exactly, so we need to decompose it into its quotient and remainder. For this, we can use synthetic division. We start by drawing up our synthetic division table:
$x^1$ $x^0$
$\color{red}-1$ $4$ $-1$
$\color{gray}\downarrow$ $-4$
$4$ $-5$
So, from the synthetic division, we get that $$ \dfrac{4x-1}{x+1} = 4 -\dfrac{5}{x+1}. $$ Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{4x-1}{x+1}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(4-\frac{5}{x+1})\,\text{d}x \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{1}4\,\text{d}x-5{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{x+1}\,\text{d}x \\ & =4x{|}_{0}^{1}-5\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+1|{|}_{0}^{1} \\ & =[4-0]-5[\operatorname{ln}⁡2-\operatorname{ln}⁡1] \\ & =4-5\operatorname{ln}⁡2.\end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186064097 :question/id #uuid "74761123-d539-5d78-8dcd-4ea1db04bed0" :question/math-academy-id "e-486" :question/problem "Calculate $$ \displaystyle\int \dfrac{2x^2-3x-4}{x-3}\,\textrm d x. $$" :question/worked-solution "We first need to decompose the integrand into its quotient and remainder parts, which we can do using synthetic division. We draw up a synthetic division table:
$x^2$ $x^1$ $x^0$
$\color{red}3$ $2$ $-3$ $-4$
$\color{gray}\downarrow$ $6$ $9$
$2$ $3$ $5$
So, from the synthetic division, we get that $$ \begin{aligned} \dfrac{ 2x^2-3x-4}{x-3} = 2x + 3 + \dfrac {5}{x-3} . \end{aligned} $$ Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned}\int \frac{2{x}^{2}-3x-4}{x-3}\,\text{d}x & =\int (2x+3+\frac{5}{x-3})\,\text{d}x \\ & ={x}^{2}+3x+5\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-3|+C.\end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186064098 :question/id #uuid "cf016fa7-c3a2-5f9b-84a6-7b005d0d7286" :question/math-academy-id "e-487" :question/problem "Evaluate $$ \displaystyle\int \dfrac{x-1}{2x-1}\,\textrm d x. $$" :question/worked-solution "First, we pull out the factor of $2$ from the denominator: $$ \begin{aligned}\int \frac{x-1}{2x-1}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{x-1}{2(x-\frac{1}{2})}\,\text{d}x \\ & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{x-1}{(x-\frac{1}{2})}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned} $$ Then, we draw up our synthetic division table to decompose the integrand into its quotient and remainder.
$x^1$ $x^0$
$\color{red}\dfrac12$ $1$ $-1$
$\color{gray}\downarrow$ $\dfrac12$
$1$ $-\dfrac12$
So, from the synthetic division, we get that $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{x-1}{(x-\frac{1}{2})} & =1-\frac{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}{(x-\frac{1}{2})} \\ & =1-\frac{1}{2(x-\frac{1}{2})} \\ & =1-\frac{1}{2x-1}.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned}\int \frac{x-1}{2x-1}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}\int (1-\frac{1}{2x-1})\,\text{d}x \\ & =\frac{1}{2}[x-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|2x-1|]+C \\ & =\frac{1}{2}x-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡|2x-1|+C.\end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186064100 :question/id #uuid "804f45cd-2082-5521-b4db-a32169716626" :question/math-academy-id "e-492" :question/problem "Calculate $$ \displaystyle\int x \cos{2x}\,\textrm d x. $$" :question/worked-solution "To solve this integral, we use the by-parts formula, given by $$ \int uv'\,\textrm{d}x= uv- \int vu'\,\textrm{d}x. $$ We need to express $\displaystyle \int x \cos{2x} \textrm{d}x$ as $\displaystyle \int uv'\,\textrm{d}x.$ Therefore, we set $$ \begin{aligned}u=x\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{cos}⁡2x\, & ⟹\,v=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x.\end{aligned} $$ We substitute the above into the integration by parts formula, and we get $$ \begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int x\operatorname{cos}⁡2x\,\text{d}x & =x\cdot \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x-\int \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x\cdot 1\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned} $$ Finally, we calculate the integral, as follows: $$ \begin{aligned}\int x\operatorname{cos}⁡2x\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}x\operatorname{sin}⁡2x-\frac{1}{2}\int \operatorname{sin}⁡2x\,\text{d}x \\ & =\frac{1}{2}x\operatorname{sin}⁡2x-\frac{1}{2}(-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x)+C \\ & =\frac{1}{2}x\operatorname{sin}⁡2x+\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+C\end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186064105 :question/id #uuid "2e0348cd-6ee1-5e95-8164-2edc58084312" :question/math-academy-id "e-558" :question/problem "Find the total finite area enclosed between the curves $y=f(x)=x^3+x^2+1$ and $y=g(x)=x^2+x+1$, as shown below. ![](images/9e/9eb2dc598188e6e9cac3a459fa41de9d2bba246e10af798fee3459d466b7f5f1.png) *(Note: Figure not drawn to scale)*" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the intersections of the two curves: $$ \begin{aligned} f(x) &= g(x) \\ x^{3} + x^{2} + 1 &= x^{2} + x + 1 \\ x^{3} - x &= 0 \\ x(x^{2} - 1) &= 0 \\ x &= 0, ± 1 \end{aligned} $$ The area we want consists of two regions: $A_1$ and $A_2$. ![](images/03/03ec1d82eb7375ce3f39a6e55d2271125d55db3fe957ac2c6a97f4dc6754de8d.png) - For the area $A_1$, we have $x \in [-1,0]$, and the upper function is $f(x)$ while the lower function is $g(x)$. So, the area is given by $$ \begin{aligned}{A}_{1} & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}(f(x)-g(x))\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}x \\ & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}(({x}^{3}+{x}^{2}+1)-({x}^{2}+x+1))\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}x \\ & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}({x}^{3}-x)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}x \\ & =(\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}){|}_{-1}^{0} \\ & =0-(\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{2}) \\ & =0-\left(-\frac{1}{4}\right) \\ & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned} $$ - For the area $A_2$, we have $x \in [0,1]$, and the upper function is $g(x)$ while the lower function is $f(x)$. So, the area is given by $$ \begin{aligned}{A}_{2} & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(g(x)-f(x))\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}x \\ & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}(({x}^{2}+x+1)-({x}^{3}+{x}^{2}+1))\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}x \\ & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{3}-x)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}x \\ & =-(\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}){|}_{0}^{1} \\ & =-(\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{2})+0 \\ & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the required area is $$ \begin{aligned} A &= A_{1} + A_{2} = \frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{4} = \frac{1}{2} \end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186064106 :question/id #uuid "a36dbf41-414c-55e3-a9f6-4b925d571442" :question/math-academy-id "e-559" :question/problem "What is the total finite area enclosed between the curves $x=y$ and $x=y^{1/7}$, as shown below? ![](images/96/96d21232b41a52516009bc756b250001b8eefb246de1c8fece3d5eb982aefe37.png)" :question/worked-solution "Let $$ \color{black}f(y)=y\, $$ and $$ \, \color{black}g(y)= y^{1/7} $$ First, we find the intersections of the two curves: $$ \begin{aligned} f(y) &= g(y) \\ y &= y^{1/7} \\ y^{7} &= y \\ y(y^{6} - 1) &= 0 \\ y(y^{3} - 1)(y^{3} + 1) &= 0 \\ y &= 0, ± 1 \end{aligned} $$ The area we want consists of two regions: $A_1$ and $A_2$. ![](images/36/3694f17ac55028c3449956601acf52f49ed840b68c47258a0b800bb56e5fd3df.png) - For the area $A_1$, we have $y \in [-1,0]$, and the right function is $f(y)$ while the left function is $g(y)$. So, the area is given by $$ \begin{aligned}{A}_{1} & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}(f(y)-g(y))\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}y \\ & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}(y-{y}^{1/7})\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}y \\ & =(\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}-\frac{7}{8}{y}^{8/7}){|}_{-1}^{0} \\ & =0-(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{7}{8}) \\ & =\frac{3}{8}.\end{aligned} $$ - For the area $A_2$, we have $y \in [0,1]$, and the right function is $g(y)$ while the left function is $f(y)$. So, the area is given by $$ \begin{aligned}{A}_{2} & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(g(y)-f(y))\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}y \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({y}^{1/7}-y)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}y \\ & =(\frac{7}{8}{y}^{8/7}-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}){|}_{0}^{1} \\ & =(\frac{7}{8}-\frac{1}{2})-0 \\ & =\frac{3}{8}.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the required area is $$ \begin{aligned} A &= A_{1} + A_{2} = \frac{3}{8} + \frac{3}{8} = \frac{3}{4} \end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186064117 :question/id #uuid "aaeb0407-771b-5dbc-8a50-e7bc0e3477c3" :question/math-academy-id "e-6209" :question/problem "Evaluate $$ \displaystyle \int_0^{\pi/5} x\sin(5x) \, \textrm{d}x. $$" :question/worked-solution "Let's use integration by parts. We set $$ \begin{aligned}u=x\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x) & ⟹\,v=-\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x).\end{aligned} $$ Substituting the above into the integration by parts formula, we get $$ \begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int x\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)\,\text{d}x & =-x\cdot \frac{1}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)-\int (-\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x))\cdot 1\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned} $$ Finally, we evaluate the integral and get $$ \begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /5}x\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)\,\text{d}x & =-{\frac{1}{5}x\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)|}_{0}^{\pi /5}+\frac{1}{5}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)\,\text{d}x \\ & =-{\frac{1}{5}x\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)|}_{0}^{\pi /5}+{\frac{1}{5}\left(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)}{5}\right)|}_{0}^{\pi /5} \\ & =[-\frac{1}{5}\cdot \frac{\pi }{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )+\frac{1}{5}\cdot 0\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(0)]+[\frac{1}{25}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )-\frac{1}{25}\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)] \\ & =[-\frac{\pi }{25}\cdot (-1)+0]+[0-0] \\ & =\frac{\pi }{25}.\end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186064128 :question/id #uuid "ceddd310-5fe4-5b55-8210-991ff22c66b0" :question/math-academy-id "e-7349" :question/problem "Peter is standing on the bank of a river. He observes a speed boat $B$ going downstream at a constant distance of $10\,\textrm{m}$ from the bank. If the boat moves at a constant speed of $8 \, \textrm{m/s}$ parallel to the bank, at what rate is the angle $\theta,$ between the observer's line of sight to the boat and the bank, decreasing when $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}6?$ Assume the angle of elevation is decreasing at a **positive** rate, and do not round the answer. ![](images/ab/abf063d149ae14c11b9ca62208a4390b32ae191418c2e0fe77f6038479fd5625.png)" :question/worked-solution "![](images/11/113109cb44fd2d10cd3b88324ed58d2ff6455a25c81b4f62eb1862b7ced03b52.png) In the figure, $y$ is the distance between the boat and the bank and $x$ is the horizontal distance traveled by that boat after passing Peter. The quantity $y=10$ meters does not change with time because the boat is at a constant distance from the bank. We wish to calculate $\dfrac{\textrm{d}\theta}{\textrm{d}t}.$ To do this, let's start by setting up a relation between $x$ and $y.$ Relative to the angle $\theta,$ the sides $x$ and $y$ are the adjacent and opposite, respectively. So, we have $$ \begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta & =\frac{y}{x} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡\theta & =\frac{10}{x} \\ x & =10\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta .\end{aligned} $$ Now, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, and we get $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(10\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta ) \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =(-10{\csc }^{2}⁡\theta )\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned} $$ From the given information, we have $\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}=8$ and $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}6.$ Substituting this into the above, we reach $$ \begin{aligned}8 & =(-10{\csc }^{2}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right))\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} \\ -\frac{4}{5} & ={\csc }^{2}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right)\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} \\ -\frac{4}{5} & ={(2)}^{2}\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} \\ -\frac{4}{5} & =4\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{1}{5}.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the rate at which the angle $\theta$ is decreasing is $\dfrac{1}{5}$ radians per second."} {:db/id 17592186064133 :question/id #uuid "5a66344e-2092-5bd6-a4d0-5663f83866b3" :question/math-academy-id "e-7556" :question/problem "A conical tank contains water. We call $H=3\,\text{m}$ the height of the tank, and $R=4\,\text{m}$ its radius at the top. These quantities are fixed and do not change with time. Now, let's consider the water level. We call $h$ the water level's height and $r$ the radius of the cone formed by the water. Both of these quantities, and the water volume $v,$ change with time. In particular, we know that $$ \dfrac{\textrm dv}{\textrm dt} = -6\pi\,\text{m}^3/\text{min}, $$ and we want to find $\dfrac{\textrm dh}{\textrm dt}$ when $h=2\,\text{m}.$ We need to find a relation between $h$ and the variable for which we know the rate of change, which is $v.$ This is given by the formula for the volume of a cone: $$ v = \dfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h $$ Before we differentiate the equation with respect to time, note that $r$ also appears in the formula. So, we need to simplify the formula by writing $r$ in terms of $h.$ Note that the cones formed by the tank and the water must be similar. Therefore, we must have $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{r}{h} & =\frac{R}{H} \\ \frac{r}{h} & =\frac{4}{3} \\ r & =\frac{4h}{3}\,.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, we can write the volume formula as $$ \begin{aligned}v & =\frac{1}{3}\pi {r}^{2}h \\ & =\frac{1}{3}\pi {\left(\frac{4h}{3}\right)}^{2}h \\ & =\frac{16}{27}\pi {h}^{3}.\end{aligned} $$ Now that we have an equation relating $v$ and $h,$ we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}v & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{16}{27}\pi {h}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{16}{9}\pi {h}^{2}\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned} $$ Finally, we plug in the known values, and we get $$ \begin{aligned}-6\pi & =\frac{16}{9}\pi ({2}^{2})\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} \\ -6\pi & =\frac{64}{9}\pi \frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{27}{32}\,\text{m/min}.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the water level is decreasing at a rate of $\dfrac{27}{32}\, \text{m/min}.$"} {:db/id 17592186064134 :question/id #uuid "3de34c88-a367-5e9f-b8de-c46953be4655" :question/math-academy-id "e-7557" :question/problem "The height of a cone is increasing at a rate of $4 \,\textrm{m}/\textrm{s}.$ The radius of the cone is always one-third of its height. So, we need to simplify the formula by writing $r$ in terms of $h.$ We're told that the diameter is $3$ times the height. So, we have $$ \begin{aligned}d & =3h \\ 2r & =3h \\ r & =\frac{3}{2}h.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, we can write the volume formula as $$ v=\frac{1}{3}\pi {(\frac{3}{2}h)}^{2}\cdot h=\frac{3}{4}\pi {h}^{3}. $$ Now that we have an equation relating just $v$ and $h,$ we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule. This gives $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}v & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{3}{4}\pi {h}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{9}{4}\pi {h}^{2}\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned} $$ Finally, substituting the known values, we get $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{9}{4}\pi (6)^{2}(5) \\ =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\cdot (\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u) \\ & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\ & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u+C \\ & Both $x$ and $y$ change with time. In particular, we know that the person's velocity is $$ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=50\,\text{in/s}. $$ Notice that the runner's velocity is positive because she is running away from the lamppost, and therefore, the distance between the runner and the lamp increases with time. Since we want to calculate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we need to find a relation between $x$ and $y.$ Since the two triangles are similar, the ratios between the corresponding sides are equal, and we have $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{x+y}{100} & =\frac{y}{60} \\ 60x+60y & =100y \\ 60x & =40y \\ y & =\frac{3}{2}x.\end{aligned} $$ We differentiate both sides of the above equation with respect to $t$ using the chain rule, and we get $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{3}{2}x) \\ & =\frac{3}{2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned} $$ Finally, substituting $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=50\,\text{in/s}$ into the above gives $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{3}{2}\cdot (50) \\ & =\frac{150}{2} \\ & =75\,\text{in/s}.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the length of the runner's shadow increases at $75\,\text{in/s}.$"} {:db/id 17592186064738 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id We want to find $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.$ To do this, let's start by setting up a relation between $x$ and $z.$ Relative to the angle $\theta =\frac{\pi }{4},$ the sides $x$ and $z$ are the adjacent and hypotenuse, respectively. So, we have $$ \begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) & =\frac{x}{z} \\ \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} & =\frac{x}{z} \\ x & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}z.\end{aligned} $$ Now, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, and we get $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}z) \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned} $$ We know that $\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}=-6\,\text{ft}/\text{s}$ (negative because the distance between the landing point and the drone is decreasing). Substituting this into the above gives $$ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\cdot (-6)=-3\sqrt{2}. $$ Therefore, the speed of the shadow is $3\sqrt{2}\,\text{ft/s}.$"} {:db/id =\frac{1}{2}(1)^{2}-\frac{2}{5}(1)^{5}+C \\ \frac{1}{10} & =\frac{1}{2}-\frac{2}{5}+C \\ C & =0.\end{aligned} $$ So the velocity is given by $$ \displaystyle v(t)=\frac{1}{2}{t}^{2}-\frac{2}{5}{t}^{5}. $$ Now, we integrate the velocity to get $x(t):$ $$ \begin{aligned}x(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\ & =\int (\frac{1}{2}{t}^{2}-\frac{2}{5}{t}^{5})\,\text{d}t \\ & =\frac{1}{6}{t}^{3}-\frac{1}{15}{t}^{6}+K\end{aligned} $$ To determine $K$, we use the fact that $x(1)=\frac{1}{10}.$ Substituting this into the
