17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "438beae6-a258-51c5-a564-575bb144d947" :question/math-academy-id "q-85823" :question/problem "The radius of the base of a cone is decreasing at a rate of $4\,\text{m}/\text{h}.$ The height of the cone is always half its radius. At what rate is the cone's volume decreasing when the radius of its base is $12\,\text{m}?$" :question/requires-calculator true :question/worked-solution "Let's call $h$ the height of the cone and $r$ the radius of its base. Both of these quantities, as well as the volume $v,$ change with time. In particular, we know that $$ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}=-4\,\text{m}/\text{h}, $$ and we need to find $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}$ when $r=12\,\text{m}.$ We need to find a relation between $v$ and the variable for which we know the rate of change, which is $r.$ This is given by the formula for the volume of a cone: $$ v=\frac{1}{3}\pi {r}^{2}h $$ Before we differentiate the equation with respect to time, note that $h$ also appears in the formula. So, we need to simplify the formula by writing $h$ in terms of $r.$ We're told that the height of the cone is half its radius. So, we have $$ \begin{aligned}h & =\frac{r}{2}.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, we can write the volume formula as $$ v=\frac{1}{3}\pi {r}^{2}\cdot \left(\frac{r}{2}\right)=\frac{1}{6}\pi {r}^{3}. $$ Now that we have an equation relating just $v$ and $r,$ we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule. This gives $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}v & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{6}\pi {r}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{1}{2}\pi {r}^{2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned} $$ Finally, substituting the known values, we get $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{1}{2}\pi (12)^{2}(-4) \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} & =-288\pi \,{\text{m}}^{3}/\text{h}.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the cone's volume is decreasing at a rate of $288\pi \,{\text{m}}^{3}/\text{h}.$"} {:db/id 17592186065353 :tutorial/content "We can prove the result $$ \displaystyle \lim_{x \to 0} \dfrac{1-\cos x}{x}=0 $$ using the limit $$ \lim_{x \to 0} \dfrac{\sin x}{x}=1 $$ First, we multiply the numerator and the denominator of $$ \dfrac{1-\cos x}{x} $$ by $1+\cos x$, and get $$ \begin{aligned} \frac{1 - \cos x}{x} &= ((1 - \cos x)(1 + \cos x))/(x(1 + \cos x)) \\ &= (1 - \cos^{2} x)/(x(1 + \cos x)) \\ &= (\sin^{2} x)/(x(1 + \cos x)) \end{aligned} $$ We now take the limit as $x\to 0$, and obtain $$ \begin{aligned} \lim_{x \to 0}\frac{1 - \cos x}{x} &= \lim_{x \to 0}(\sin^{2} x)/(x(1 + \cos x)) \\ &= \lim_{x \to 0}(\frac{\sin x}{x} \cdot \frac{\sin x}{1 + \cos x}) \\ &= (\lim_{x \to 0}\frac{\sin x}{x}) \cdot (\lim_{x \to 0}\frac{\sin x}{1 + \cos x}) \\ &= 1 \cdot \frac{\sin 0}{1 + \cos 0} \\ &= \frac{0}{1 + 1} \\ &= 0 \end{aligned} $$" :tutorial/id #uuid "bf4486ad-5107-5bcf-b7f3-d8c6ce7a05a5" :tutorial/math-academy-id 286 :tutorial/title "Proof of the Limit"} {:db/id 17592186065372 :tutorial/content "To compute the integral of any power function $x^n,$ where $n \neq -1,$ we can use the **power rule for integration**. The power rule for integration states that $$ \int x^n\, \textrm{d}x = \dfrac {x^{n + 1}}{n + 1} + C, $$ where $C$ is any constant and $n\neq -1.$ For example, in the case of $n=3,$ we have $$ \begin{aligned}\int {x}^{3}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{{x}^{3+1}}{3+1}+C \\ & =\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}+C.\end{aligned} $$ So the **antiderivative** of $f'(x) = x^3$ is $f(x) = \dfrac {x^{4}}{4}+C .$ We can check that this is the correct answer by taking the derivative of $f(x)$ and seeing that it is indeed equal to $x^3\mathbin{:}$ $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}+C) &= \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\left(\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}\right)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) \\ &= \frac{1}{4}(\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}{x}^{4})+0 \\ &= \frac{1}{4}\cdot 4{x}^{4-1} \\ &= {x}^{3}\hspace{1em}{\color{green}✓}\end{aligned} $$ Notice that the constant $C$ disappeared when we differentiated because the derivative of any constant is zero. We always add $+C$ whenever we find the antiderivative of a function because we know that it will disappear when we differentiate. **Note:** The power rule for integration is just the power rule for differentiation in reverse! $$ \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x} \left( x^{n+1} \right) = (n+1)x^n \quad \Leftrightarrow \quad \displaystyle \int x^n \, \textrm dx = \dfrac{x^{n+1}}{n+1} $$" :tutorial/id #uuid "9f08a264-7a79-50c1-afb0-903bb2a256f1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3852 :tutorial/title "The Power Rule for Integration"} {:db/id 17592186065373 :tutorial/content "We can use our special limit with cosine to evaluate other limits, such as $$ \lim_{x \to 3} \dfrac{1-\cos(x-3)}{2x-6} $$ For this limit, notice that as $x\to3$, both the numerator and denominator approach $0$. So, if we attempt to evaluate the limit directly, we get $$ \dfrac00, $$ which is an indeterminate form. Instead, we rewrite the limit using the algebra of limits, as follows: $$ \begin{aligned} \lim_{x \to 3}(1 - \cos (x - 3))/(2x - 6) &= \lim_{x \to 3}(1 - \cos (x - 3))/(2(x - 3)) \\ &= \lim_{x \to 3}(\frac{1}{2} \cdot (1 - \cos (x - 3))/(x - 3)) \\ &= \frac{1}{2} \cdot lim_(x → 3)(1 - \cos (x - 3))/((x - 3)) \end{aligned} $$ Now, this limit looks very similar to our special limit for cosine. So, if we make the substitution $$ \theta = x-3 $$ then, since $\theta \to 0$ as $x \to 3$, we have $$ \lim_{x \to 3} \dfrac{1-\cos{\color{blue}(x-3)}}{\color{blue}(x-3)} = \lim_{\theta \to 0} \: \dfrac{1-\cos {\color{blue}\theta}}{\color{blue}\theta} = 0 $$ Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned} \lim_{x \to 3}(1 - \cos (x - 3))/(2x - 6) &= \frac{1}{2} \cdot lim_(x → 3)(1 - \cos (x - 3))/((x - 3)) \\ &= \frac{1}{2} \cdot 0 \\ &= 0 \end{aligned} $$" :tutorial/id #uuid "f89c2a3a-09f1-557f-a00d-5a98b6a93684" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3894 :tutorial/title "Special Limits Involving Cosine Using a Substitution"} {:db/id 17592186065387 :tutorial/content "Suppose that a jet takes off and climbs with an angle of $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ radians to the horizontal. The speed of the jet is $462\,\text{km}/\text{h}$ and the angle of elevation does not change. How fast is the altitude of the jet increasing? Let's begin by drawing a diagram depicting the given information. ![](images/70/708ba0a80dd7c8e3e58e1456ad643338a8e630ec45aedb8955b042ddac92c329.png) In the figure, $y$ is the jet's height from the ground (i.e., its altitude), $z$ is the jet's distance from its take-off point. The quantity that we're required to calculate is $$ \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}. $$ To do this, let's start by setting up a relation between $y$ and $z.$ Relative to the angle $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{6},$ the sides $y$ and $z$ are the opposite and hypotenuse, respectively. So, we have $$ \begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right) & =\frac{y}{z} \\ \frac{1}{2} & =\frac{y}{z} \\ y & =\frac{1}{2}z.\end{aligned} $$ Now, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $t$ using the chain rule, and we get $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{2}z) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{1}{2}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned} $$ We know that $\dfrac{\textrm d z}{\textrm d t} = 462\,\textrm{km/h},$ so plugging this into the above gives $$ \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t} = \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot 462 = 231. $$ Therefore, the altitude is increasing at a rate of $231\,\textrm{km/h}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "da3b2021-8bcc-506c-8874-9ce60aca7594" :tutorial/math-academy-id 501 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186065396 :tutorial/content "When a function $y=y(x)$ contains complex products, quotients, or radicals, we can use logarithmic differentiation to find the derivative $y'(x).$ For example, consider the following function: $$ y = x^2 \cdot 2^x $$ Our goal is to find $y'(x).$ To do this, we will use the product rule for logarithms, namely $$ \ln(a b)= \ln a + \ln b. $$ We differentiate our function by following four steps. **Step 1.** We take the natural logarithm of both sides and apply the product and power rules: $$ \begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}\cdot {2}^{x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})+\operatorname{ln}⁡({2}^{x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡x+x\operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{aligned} $$ **Step 2.** Next, we differentiate both sides of our equation using implicit differentiation: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2\operatorname{ln}⁡x+x\operatorname{ln}⁡2) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =2\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{′}+(x)^{′}\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(2) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =2\cdot \frac{1}{x}+1\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(2) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\frac{2}{x}+\operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{aligned} $$ **Step 3.** Then, we solve for $y'{:}$ $$ \begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(\frac{2}{x}+\operatorname{ln}⁡2)\end{aligned} $$ **Step 4.** Finally, we substitute back our original expression for $y =x^2\cdot 2^x{:}$ $$ \begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & ={x}^{2}\cdot {2}^{x}(\frac{2}{x}+\operatorname{ln}⁡2) \\ & =x\cdot {2}^{x+1}+{x}^{2}\cdot {2}^{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{aligned} $$" :tutorial/id #uuid "1895a7f3-5ba4-5a31-85b3-6a7b050b307c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6088 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186065397 :tutorial/content "In cases where we wish to differentiate a quotient of functions $$ y = f(x) = \dfrac{g(x)}{h(x)}, $$ we can apply the quotient rule for logarithms: $$ \ln \left(\dfrac{a}{b}\right) = \ln a - \ln b $$ For example, let's compute $y',$ where the function $y$ is given by $$ y = \dfrac {e^{x^2}}{(1-2x)^2(x-1)^3}. $$ First, we find the natural logarithm of both sides and use the quotient and power rules for logarithms: $$ \begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{{e}^{{x}^{2}}}{(1-2x)^{2}(x-1)^{3}}\right) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{{x}^{2}})-\operatorname{ln}⁡((1-2x)^{2})-\operatorname{ln}⁡((x-1)^{3}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & ={x}^{2}-2\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-2x)-3\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-1)\end{aligned} $$ Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x{:}$ $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}-2\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-2x)-3\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-1)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =2x-2\cdot \frac{1}{1-2x}\cdot (-2)-3\cdot \frac{1}{x-1} \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =2x+\frac{4}{1-2x}-\frac{3}{x-1}\end{aligned} $$ Now, we solve for $y'{:}$ $$ \begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(2x+\frac{4}{1-2x}-\frac{3}{x-1})\end{aligned} $$ Finally, we substitute our expression for $y,$ and simplify: $$ \begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{{e}^{{x}^{2}}}{(1-2x)^{2}(x-1)^{3}}(2x+\frac{4}{1-2x}-\frac{3}{x-1}) \\ & =\frac{{e}^{{x}^{2}}}{(1-2x)^{2}(x-1)^{3}}\left(\frac{2x(1-2x)(x-1)+4(x-1)-3(1-2x)}{(1-2x)(x-1)}\right) \\ & =\frac{{e}^{{x}^{2}}}{(1-2x)^{3}(x-1)^{4}}(2x(1-2x)(x-1)+4(x-1)-3(1-2x)) \\ & =\frac{{e}^{{x}^{2}}}{(1-2x)^{3}(x-1)^{4}}(-4{x}^{3}+6{x}^{2}+8x-7) \\ & =-\frac{{e}^{{x}^{2}}}{(1-2x)^{3}(x-1)^{4}}(4{x}^{3}-6{x}^{2}-8x+7) \\ & =-\frac{{e}^{{x}^{2}}(4{x}^{3}-6{x}^{2}-8x+7)}{(1-2x)^{3}(x-1)^{4}}\end{aligned} $$" :tutorial/id #uuid "8cf6e625-669a-5fda-b756-e1ce091eaa93" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6090 :tutorial/title "Using Logarithms to Differentiate a Quotient"} {:db/id 17592186065424 :tutorial/content "We know how to calculate $$ \displaystyle\int x^5 \, \textrm{d}x. $$ But suppose that we want to calculate an integral like $$ \int (2x+1)^5 \, \textrm{d}x. $$ The integral above is different from what we've seen previously because now it's a whole function $(2x+1)$ that is being raised to the power of $5.$ So what do we do? In this case, the answer is to introduce a new variable. Our goal is to replace all of the $x$'s in the integral, *including* the $\textrm d x$, with this new variable which we'll call $u.$ First, we let $u=2x+1.$ Differentiating both sides with respect to $x$ gives $$ \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = 2, $$ and if we treat $\dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x}$ like a fraction, we can get the $\textrm d x$ on its own as $$ \textrm{d} x = \dfrac 1 2 \textrm d u. $$ We're now in a position to write our integral in terms of the new variable $u,$ which we do as follows: $$ \begin{aligned}\int (2x+1)^{5}\,\text{d}x & =\int {u}^{5}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{d}u \\ & =\frac{1}{2}\int {u}^{5}\text{d}u.\end{aligned} $$ We now calculate our integral as normal, and write the final answer in terms of $x$ at the very end: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\int {u}^{5}\text{d}u & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{{u}^{6}}{6}+C \\ & =\frac{1}{12}{u}^{6}+C \\ & =\frac{1}{12}(2x+1)^{6}+C.\end{aligned} $$ **Note:** After solving an integral using substitution, we should always double-check that our result is correct. If we differentiate the result, then it should come out to the original integrand: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[\frac{1}{12}(2x+1)^{6}+C] & =\frac{1}{12}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[(2x+1)^{6}]+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) \\ & =\frac{1}{12}\cdot 6(2x+1)^{5}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2x+1)+0 \\ & =\frac{1}{2}(2x+1)^{5}\cdot 2 \\ & =(2x+1)^{5}\,✓\end{aligned} $$" :tutorial/id #uuid "bab59a0d-1a9b-5dd6-a00f-750a020fbbb6" :tutorial/math-academy-id 825 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186065428 :tutorial/content "Suppose that we want to calculate an integral like $$ \displaystyle \int \dfrac{1}{2x+1} \, \textrm{d}x. $$ We know that $$ \displaystyle \int \dfrac{1}{x} \, \textrm dx = \ln |x|, $$ but our case is different because now it's a whole function $(2x+1)$ that is in the denominator. For integrals like the one above, we can use a substitution. First, let $u=2x+1.$ Then differentiating with respect to $x$ gives $$ \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = 2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm d x = \dfrac 1 2 \, \textrm d u. $$ We can now rewrite the integral in terms of $u$ and solve it: $$ \begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{2x+1}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\ & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\ & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}|u|+C\end{aligned} $$ Lastly, we write the final answer in terms of $x$: $$ \begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{2x+1}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}|2x+1|+C\end{aligned} $$ **Note:** After solving an integral using substitution, we should always double-check that our result is correct. If we differentiate the result, then it should come out to the original integrand: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}|2x+1|+C] & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[\operatorname{ln}|2x+1|]+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) \\ & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2x+1}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2x+1)+0 \\ & =\frac{1}{2(2x+1)}\cdot 2 \\ & =\frac{1}{2x+1}\,✓\end{aligned} $$" :tutorial/id #uuid "539b2d2a-d59d-59a2-8b1b-cd7fbe582c04" :tutorial/math-academy-id 830 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186065433 :tutorial/content "Consider the integral $$ \int \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1-4x^2}} \, \textrm{d}x. $$ This integral, apart from the coefficient of $4$ in the denominator, resembles the basic integral $$ \int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-u^2}}\textrm{d}u = \arcsin(u)+C. $$ In fact, they look almost the same, but instead of $u^2$ as the variable, we have $4x^2 = (2x)^2.$ So, let's substitute $u=2x.$ Differentiating, we get $$ \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac 1 2 \textrm d u = \textrm d x. $$ We can now write the integral in terms of $u,$ and evaluate: $$ \begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-4{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(2x)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\ & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\ & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\ & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(u)+C \\ & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(2x)+C.\end{aligned} $$ We can often use this trick whenever we see an integral that closely resembles an integral for an inverse trigonometric function. **Note:** As always, after solving an integral using substitution, we should always double-check that our result is correct. If we differentiate the result, then it should come out to the original integrand: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(2x)+C] & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(2x)]+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) \\ & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(2x)^{2}}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2x)+0 \\ & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-4{x}^{2}}}\cdot 2 \\ & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-4{x}^{2}}}\,✓\end{aligned} $$" :tutorial/id #uuid "53af5e98-4580-5243-a97c-de9e0d5f8fab" :tutorial/math-academy-id 863 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186065438 :tutorial/content "How do we calculate $$ \displaystyle \int\dfrac{3x+2}{x+2}\,\textrm d x\,? $$ We need to write the integrand so that it's something we can integrate. One way to do this is to divide $3x+2$ by $x+2$ using polynomial or synthetic division. We'll use synthetic division because it's faster. To rewrite $\dfrac{3x+2}{x+2},$ we complete a synthetic division table.
$x^1$ $x^0$
$\color{red}-2$ $3$ $2$
$\color{gray}\downarrow$ $-6$
$3$ $-4$
This tells us that $\dfrac{3x+2}{x+2}$ can be decomposed into a quotient and remainder as $$ \dfrac{3x+2}{x+2}= 3 - \dfrac{4}{x+2}. $$ Now, we can integrate the function, which gives $$ \begin{aligned}\int \frac{3x+2}{x+2}\,\text{d}x & =\int (3-\frac{4}{x+2})\,\text{d}x \\ & =\int 3\,\text{d}x-4\int \frac{1}{x+2}\,\text{d}x \\ & =3x-4\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+2|+C.\end{aligned} $$" :tutorial/id #uuid "2437a8a0-d1de-5b85-8577-7e7493c4d520" :tutorial/math-academy-id 884 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186065447 :tutorial/content "Consider the following function: $$ f(x)= 4x^2+x, \qquad x \gt 0 $$ The domain restriction $x > 0$ means that $f$ is invertible on its entire domain. The point $P$ with coordinates $(2,18)$ lies on the curve $y = f(x).$ This means that the point $P'$ with coordinates $(18,2)$ lies on the curve of the inverse function $y=f^{-1}(x),$ as shown below. ![](images/3e/3e16e532743be547c766e5a6a47bae8933a8dedb2b6d0fa0d60d47cc0b37ba04.png) How do we find $\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x}$ at the point $P'?$ For this, we will use the fact that the slope of the tangent to the curve $y=f^{-1}(x)$ at $P'$ is the *reciprocal* of the slope of the tangent to the curve $y=f(x)$ at $P.$ $$ \begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{{P}^{′}} &=\frac{1}{({\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{P})}\end{aligned} $$ Calculating $\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x}$ at $P$ is straightforward. First, we differentiate $y=f(x).$ This gives $$ \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = 8x + 1, $$ and then plugging in $x=2$ gives $$ \left.\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}\right|_P = 8(2)+1 = 17. $$ Finally, we take the reciprocal: $$ \left.\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}\right|_{P'}= \dfrac{1}{17} $$ We can summarize this process using the following formula: $$ \left(f^{-1}\right)'(x) = \dfrac{1}{f'(f^{-1}(x))} $$ To help remember this formula, note that it's okay to swap the derivative symbol (the prime) with the inverse symbol (the exponent of $-1$) as long as we take the reciprocal afterward." :tutorial/id #uuid "a1f70bcd-9b56-5fdd-ba18-58b625c05af0" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9132 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:answer/id #uuid "bb2585a3-a664-54da-8d5b-b239545056fd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(\frac{2}{3}, 0)" :db/id 17592186066583} {:answer/id #uuid "c338bc12-0ff7-5a76-a030-be58a3ab86eb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(0, \frac{2}{3})" :db/id 17592186066584} {:answer/id #uuid "d00aa293-bf91-5633-90dd-7eed6a5053fb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(0, \frac{5}{3})" :db/id 17592186066585} {:answer/id #uuid "ccaf6707-73e5-566c-aefc-940bbcf90e54" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "k ∈ (- ∞,-\frac{1}{2})" :db/id 17592186067193} {:answer/id #uuid "c3ce49ce-6a53-5b83-9564-106f32f18abd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨2, \frac{1}{2}⟩" :db/id 17592186067643} {:answer/id #uuid "c5d8be60-3856-5e3f-b942-67b33c088ce5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{2}⟩" :db/id 17592186067644} {:answer/id #uuid "10246158-ec52-5f5e-aaae-27da3f8bd289" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨\frac{1}{2}, 2⟩" :db/id 17592186067647} {:answer/id #uuid "ade7268a-6371-596d-aed8-1afa2a8e3e81" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(2 - So, we set up the two corresponding equations and solve them independently: - If $$ \displaystyle \left| \dfrac{7}{2}z-2 \right| = \dfrac{7}{2}z-2, $$ we obtain: $$ \begin{aligned}|\frac{7}{2}z-2| & =3 \\ \frac{7}{2}z-2 & =3 \\ \frac{7}{2}z & =5\end{aligned} $$ Multiplying both sides of the equation by $\dfrac{2}{7}$ gives $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{7}{2}z & =5 \\ \left(\frac{2}{7}\right)\cdot (\frac{7}{2}z) & =\left(\frac{2}{7}\right)\cdot (5) \\ (\cancel{\frac{2}{7}})\cdot (\cancel{\frac{7}{2}}z) & =\frac{10}{7} \\ z & =\frac{10}{7}.\end{aligned} $$ - If $$ \displaystyle \left| \dfrac{7}{2}z-2 \right| = -\left(\dfrac{7}{2}z-2\right), $$ we obtain: $$ \begin{aligned}|\frac{7}{2}z-2| & =3 \\ -(\frac{7}{2}z-2) & =3 \\ -\frac{7}{2}z+2 & =3 \\ -\frac{7}{2}z & =1\end{aligned} $$ Multiplying both sides of the equation by $-\dfrac{2}{7}$ gives $$ \begin{aligned}-\frac{7}{2}z & =1 \\ \left(-\frac{2}{7}\right)\cdot (-\frac{7}{2}z) & =\left(-\frac{2}{7}\right)\cdot (1) \\ (\cancel{-\frac{2}{7}})\cdot (\cancel{-\frac{7}{2}}z) & =-\frac{2}{7} \\ z & =-\frac{2}{7}.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the solutions are $z = -\dfrac{2}{7}$ and $z = \dfrac{10}{7}.$"} {:db/id 17592186068563 :question/id #uuid "fd2d4aca-7859-5bed-a514-43d82ba25400" :question/math-academy-id "e-4102" :question/problem "Calculate $$ \displaystyle \int \dfrac{2x+3}{(x^2+4)(x-1)} \, \textrm{d}x. $$" :question/worked-solution "The quadratic factor $x^2+4$ is irreducible, so we proceed with the following partial fraction decomposition: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{2x+3}{({x}^{2}+4)(x-1)} & =\frac{Ax+B}{({x}^{2}+4)}+\frac{C}{(x-1)}\end{aligned} $$ To determine the coefficients $A,$ $B,$ and $C,$ we first multiply both sides of the above equation by $(x^2+4)(x-1),$ and we get $$ \begin{aligned}2x+3 & =(Ax+B)(x-1)+C({x}^{2}+4)\,.\end{aligned} $$ Solving for the unknown constants using the usual methods, we get $A=-1, B=1,$ and $C=1.$ Therefore, $$ \dfrac{2x+3}{(x^2+4)(x-1)} = \dfrac{-x+1}{x^2+4} +\dfrac{1}{x-1}. $$ Now we integrate this function term by term, adding the constant of integration at the very end. $$ \begin{aligned}\int \frac{2x+3}{({x}^{2}+4)(x-1)}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{-x+1}{{x}^{2}+4}+\frac{1}{x-1})\text{d}x \\ & =-\int \frac{x}{{x}^{2}+4}\,\text{d}x+\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+4}\,\text{d}x+\int \frac{1}{x-1}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned} $$ For the first integral, we use the substitution $u = x^2+4.$ Then $2x\,\textrm{d}x=\textrm{d}u,$ and we get $$ \begin{aligned}\int \frac{x}{{x}^{2}+4}\,\text{d}x & =\int \left(\frac{1}{u}\right)\frac{\text{d}u}{2} \\ & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|u| \\ & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|{x}^{2}+4| \\ & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+4).\end{aligned} $$ For the second integral, we use the fact that $$ \displaystyle \int \dfrac{1}{x^2+a^2} \, \textrm{d}x = \dfrac{1}{a}\arctan\left(\dfrac{x}{a}\right), $$ which results in $$ \begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+4}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡\left(\frac{x}{2}\right).\end{aligned} $$ Finally, for the third integral we have $$ \begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{x-1}\text{d}x & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-1|.\end{aligned} $$ So we get the following result: $$ \begin{aligned}\int \frac{2x+3}{({x}^{2}+4)(x-1)}\,\text{d}x & =-\int \frac{x}{{x}^{2}+4}\,\text{d}x+\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+4}\,\text{d}x+\int \frac{1}{x-1}\,\text{d}x \\ & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+4)+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)+\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-1|+K\end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186068568 :question/id #uuid "daf5cc74-4c7d-500a-9345-03bd6b73a333" :question/math-academy-id "e-465" :question/problem "Calculate the integral $$ \displaystyle\int 5 \csc {\left(6x+\dfrac \pi 3\right)} \cot {\left(6x+\dfrac \pi 3\right)} \, \textrm{d}x. $$" :question/worked-solution "If we let $u=6x+\dfrac \pi 3,$ then $$ \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = 6\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm d x =\dfrac 1 6\, \textrm d u. $$ Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate: $$ \begin{aligned}\int 5\operatorname{csc}⁡(6x+\frac{\pi }{3})\operatorname{cot}⁡(6x+\frac{\pi }{3})\,\text{d}x & =5\int \operatorname{csc}⁡(6x+\frac{\pi }{3})\operatorname{cot}⁡(6x+\frac{\pi }{3})\,\text{d}x \\ & =5\int \operatorname{csc}⁡u\operatorname{cot}⁡u\cdot \frac{1}{6}\,\text{d}u \\ & =\frac{5}{6}\int \operatorname{csc}⁡u\operatorname{cot}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\ & =-\frac{5}{6}\operatorname{csc}⁡u+C \\ & =-\frac{5}{6}\operatorname{csc}⁡(6x+\frac{\pi }{3})+C\end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186068569 $$" :question/worked-solution "Let $u = x^3 - \dfrac{\pi}{6}.$ Differentiating, we have $$ \dfrac{\textrm{d} u}{\textrm{d}x } = 3x^2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac 1 3 \textrm d u = x^2\,\textrm d }{6})\cdot {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\ & =\int {\sec }^{2}⁡(u)\cdot \frac{1}{3}\,\text{d}u \\ & =\frac{1}{3}\int {\sec }^{2}⁡(u)\,\text{d}u \\ & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{tan}⁡u+C \\ & Using the formula for integration by parts, we get $$ \begin{aligned}\int {x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\text{d}x \\ & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\text{d}x \\ & =({x}^{2})(\frac{1}{3}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x))-\int (\frac{1}{3}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x))2x\,\text{d}x \\ & =\frac{1}{3}{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)-\frac{2}{3}\int x\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\text{d}x.\end{aligned} $$ Again, we use integration by parts to evaluate $$ \displaystyle \int x\sin(3x) \operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\text{d}x=-\,\frac{1}{3}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,.\end{aligned} $$ In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives $$ \begin{aligned}\int x\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\text{d}x \\ & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\text{d}x \\ & =x(-\,\frac{1}{3}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x))-\int In this case, we define $$ \begin{aligned}u=(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{2} & \,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=32{x}^{3} & \,⟹\,v=\int 32{x}^{3}\text{d}x=8{x}^{4}\,.\end{aligned} $$ Using the formula of integration by parts, we get $$ \begin{aligned}\int 32{x}^{3}(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{2}\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\text{d}x \\ & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\text{d}x \\ & ={(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}(8{x}^{4})-\int (8{x}^{4})\left(\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x}\right)\text{d}x \\ & =8{x}^{4}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}-16\int {x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)\text{d}x.\end{aligned} $$ We use integration by parts once again to evaluate $$ \displaystyle\int {x^3\ln(x)} \textrm{d}x. $$ We take $$ \begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x) & \,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}={x}^{3} & \,⟹\,v=\int {x}^{3}\text{d}x=\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}\,.\end{aligned} $$ In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives $$ \begin{aligned}\int {x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\text{d}x \\ & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\text{d}x \\ & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)\left(\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}\right)-\int \left(\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}\right)\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)\text{d}x \\ & =\frac{{x}^{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}{4}-\frac{1}{4}\int {x}^{3}\text{d}x \\ & =\frac{{x}^{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}{4}-\frac{{x}^{4}}{16}+{C}_{1}\end{aligned} $$ where $C_1$ is an integral constant. So, we get that the indefinite integral is $$ \begin{aligned}\int 32{x}^{3}(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{2}\text{d}x & =8{x}^{4}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}-16\int {x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)\text{d}x \\ & =8{x}^{4}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}-16(\frac{{x}^{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}{4}-\frac{{x}^{4}}{16}+{C}_{1}) \\ & =8{x}^{4}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}-4{x}^{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)+{x}^{4}-16{C}_{1} \\ & ={x}^{4}(8{(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}-4\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)+1)+C\,\end{aligned} $$ where $C = -4C_1.$ Finally then, we can work out the definite integral: $$ \begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{e}32{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)\text{d}x & ={{x}^{4}(8{(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}-4\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)+1)|}_{1}^{e} \\ & =[(e)^{4}(8{(\operatorname{ln}⁡(e))}^{2}-4\operatorname{ln}⁡(e)+1)]-[(1)^{4}(8{(\operatorname{ln}⁡(1))}^{2}-4\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)+1)] \\ & =[{e}^{4}(8-4+1)]-1 \\ & =5{e}^{4}-1.\end{aligned} $$"} :question/problem "Evaluate $$ \displaystyle \int \dfrac{5x}{x^2+3x-4} \,\textrm{d}x. $$" :question/worked-solution "First, we note that the denominator of the integrand can be factored as $$ x^2+3x-4 = (x-1)(x+4) \,. $$ So, the integrand can be converted into a sum of partial fractions, $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{5x}{{x}^{2}+3x-4} & =\frac{5x}{(x-1)(x+4)} \\ & =\frac{A}{(x-1)}+\frac{B}{(x+4)},\end{aligned} $$ which gives $$ \begin{aligned}5x & =A(x+4)+B(x-1).\end{aligned} $$ Plugging in $x=-4,$ we can eliminate $A$ and solve for $B\mathbin{:}$ $$ \begin{aligned}5(-4) & =A(-4+4)+B(-4-1) \\ -20 & =-5B \\ B & =4.\end{aligned} $$ On the other hand, by plugging in $x=1,$ we can eliminate $B$ and solve for $A\mathbin{:}$ $$ \begin{aligned}5(1) & =A(1+4)+B(1-1) \\ 5 & =5A \\ A & =1.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, $$ \dfrac{5x}{x^2+3x-4} = \dfrac{1}{(x-1)} +\dfrac{4}{(x+4)}. $$ Finally, we integrate, and we get $$ \begin{aligned}\int \frac{5x}{{x}^{2}+3x-4}\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{1}{x-1}+\frac{4}{x+4})\text{d}x \\ & =\int \frac{1}{x-1}\text{d}x+4\int \frac{1}{x+4}\text{d}x \\ & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-1|+4\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+4|+C.\end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186068586 :question/id #uuid "fce14198-c8ee-50a6-981d-85df79cce761" :question/math-academy-id "e-507" :question/problem "Evaluate $$ \displaystyle \int_1^4 \dfrac{2x+3}{4x^2-1} \,\textrm{d}x. $$" :question/worked-solution "We'll work out the indefinite integral first and then proceed with the definite integral. First, we note that a denominator of the integrand can be factored as $$ 4x^2-1 = (2x+1)(2x-1) \,. $$ So the integrand can be converted into a sum of partial fractions, $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{2x+3}{4{x}^{2}-1} & =\frac{2x+3}{(2x+1)(2x-1)} \\ & =\frac{A}{(2x+1)}+\frac{B}{(2x-1)},\end{aligned} $$ which gives $$ \begin{aligned}2x+3 & =A(2x-1)+B(2x+1).\end{aligned} $$ Plugging in $x=\dfrac{1}{2},$ we can eliminate $A$ and solve for $B\mathbin{:}$ $$ \begin{aligned}2\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)+3 & =A(2\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)-1)+B(2\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)+1) \\ 4 & =2B \\ B & =2.\end{aligned} $$ On the other hand, plugging in $x=-\dfrac{1}{2},$ we can eliminate $B$ and solve for $A\mathbin{:}$ $$ \begin{aligned}2\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)+3 & =A(2\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)-1)+B(2\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)+1) \\ 2 & =-2A \\ A & =-1.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, $$ \dfrac{2x+3}{4x^2-1} = -\dfrac{1}{(2x+1)} +\dfrac{2}{(2x-1)}. $$ Now, we integrate and get $$ \begin{aligned}\int \frac{2x+3}{4{x}^{2}-1}\text{d}x & =\int (-\frac{1}{(2x+1)}+\frac{2}{(2x-1)})\text{d}x \\ & =-\int \frac{1}{2x+1}\text{d}x+2\int \frac{1}{2x-1}\text{d}x \\ & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|2x+1|+2(\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|2x-1|)+C \\ & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|2x+1|+\operatorname{ln}⁡|2x-1|+C.\end{aligned} $$ We can simplify the result using the laws of logarithms, as follows: $$ \begin{aligned}\int \frac{2x+3}{4{x}^{2}-1}\text{d}x & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|2x+1|+\operatorname{ln}⁡|2x-1|+C \\ & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|\frac{1}{\sqrt{2x+1}}|+\operatorname{ln}⁡|2x-1|+C \\ & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|\frac{2x-1}{\sqrt{2x+1}}|+C\end{aligned} $$ Finally, the definite integral is $$ \begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{2x+3}{4{x}^{2}-1}\,\text{d}x & =\operatorname{ln}⁡{|\frac{2x-1}{\sqrt{2x+1}}|}_{1}^{4} \\ & =\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{7}{3}\right)-\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right) \\ & =\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{7}{3}\right)+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{3}) \\ & =\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{7\sqrt{3}}{3}\right).\end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186068587 :question/id #uuid "2fb19e4b-c455-599f-8856-5bee85f8efc4" :question/math-academy-id "e-508" :question/problem "Calculate $$ \displaystyle \int_0^1 \dfrac{2x+3}{(x+1)^2} \,\textrm{d}x. $$" :question/worked-solution "First, we convert the integrand into a sum of partial fractions: $$ \dfrac{2x+3}{(x+1)^2} = \dfrac{A}{(x+1)} +\dfrac{B}{(x+1)^2} $$ To determine the coefficients $A,$ and $B,$ we first multiply both sides of the above equation by $(x+1)^2$ and get $$ 2x+3 = A(x+1)+B . $$ Plugging in $x=-1,$ we can eliminate $A$ and solve for $B\mathbin{:}$ $$ \begin{aligned}2(-1)+3 & =A(-1+1)+B \\ 1 & =0+B \\ B & =1\end{aligned} $$ Now, plugging in $x=0$ and substituting the known value of $B,$ we can solve for $A\mathbin{:}$ $$ \begin{aligned}2(0)+3 & =A(0+1)+B \\ 3 & =A+B \\ 3 & =A+1 \\ A & =2\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, we can write the integrand as the partial sum $$ \dfrac{2x+3}{(x+1)^2} = \dfrac{2}{(x+1)} +\dfrac{1}{(x+1)^2}. $$ Finally, we integrate this expression term by term to get $$ \begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{2x+3}{(x+1)^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{2}{(x+1)}+\frac{1}{(x+1)^{2}})\,\text{d}x \\ & =2{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{x+1}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{(x+1)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\ & =2{\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+1||}_{0}^{1}+{\left(-\frac{1}{x+1}\right)|}_{0}^{1} \\ & =2{\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+1||}_{0}^{1}-{\frac{1}{x+1}|}_{0}^{1} \\ & =2[\operatorname{ln}⁡2-\operatorname{ln}⁡1]-[\frac{1}{2}-1] \\ & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡2+\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186068588 :question/id #uuid "789c5233-a263-55a7-9b27-c834b2ceaf8d" :question/math-academy-id "e-509" :question/problem "Evaluate $$ \displaystyle \int \dfrac{9x^2+2x-1}{(3x-1)^3}\textrm{d}x. $$" :question/worked-solution "First, we convert the integrand into a sum of partial fractions: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{9{x}^{2}+2x-1}{(3x-1)^{3}} & =\frac{A}{(3x-1)}+\frac{B}{(3x-1)^{2}}+\frac{C}{(3x-1)^{3}}\end{aligned} $$ To determine the coefficients $A,$ $B,$ and $C,$ we first multiply both sides of the above equation by $(3x-1)^3$ and get $$ \begin{aligned}9{x}^{2}+2x-1 & =A(3x-1)^{2}+B(3x-1)+C.\end{aligned} $$ Plugging in $x=\dfrac{1}{3},$ we can eliminate $A$ and $B$ and solve for $C\mathbin{:}$ $$ \begin{aligned}9{\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)}^{2}+2\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)-1 & =A{(3\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)-1)}^{2}+B(3\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)-1)+C \\ C & =\frac{2}{3}\end{aligned} $$ Plugging in $x=0$ and substituting the known value of $C,$ we get an equation relating $A$ and $B\mathbin{:}$ $$ \begin{aligned}9{(0)}^{2}+2(0)-1 & =A{(0-1)}^{2}+B(0-1)+C \\ -1 & =A-B+\frac{2}{3} \\ A-B & =-\frac{5}{3}\end{aligned} $$ Plugging in $x=1$ and substituting the known value of $C,$ we get another equation relating $A$ and $B\mathbin{:}$ $$ \begin{aligned}9{(1)}^{2}+2(1)-1 & =A{(3(1)-1)}^{2}+B(3(1)-1)+C \\ 10 & =4A+2B+\frac{2}{3} \\ 2A+B & =\frac{14}{3}\end{aligned} $$ Adding our two equations $A-B=-\dfrac{5}{3}$ and $2A+B=\dfrac{14}{3},$ we get $$ \begin{aligned}3A & =-\frac{5}{3}+\frac{14}{3} \\ 3A & =3 \\ A & =1,\end{aligned} $$ and substituting back into $2A+B=\dfrac{14}{3},$ we get $$ \begin{aligned}2(1)+B & =\frac{14}{3} \\ B & =\frac{8}{3}.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, $$ \dfrac{9x^2+2x-1}{(3x-1)^3} = \dfrac{1}{(3x-1)} +\dfrac{8}{3(3x-1)^2} + \dfrac{2}{3(3x-1)^3}. $$ Finally, we integrate this expression term by term, and get $$ \begin{aligned}\int \frac{9{x}^{2}+2x-1}{(3x-1)^{3}}\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{1}{(3x-1)}+\frac{8}{3(3x-1)^{2}}+\frac{2}{3(3x-1)^{3}})\text{d}x \\ & =\int \frac{1}{3x-1}\text{d}x+\frac{8}{3}\int \frac{1}{(3x-1)^{2}}\text{d}x+\frac{2}{3}\int \frac{1}{(3x-1)^{3}}\text{d}x \\ & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡|3x-1|+\frac{8}{3}(-\,\frac{1}{3(3x-1)})+\frac{2}{3}(-\,\frac{1}{6(3x-1)^{2}})+K \\ & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡|3x-1|-\frac{8}{9(3x-1)}-\frac{1}{9(3x-1)^{2}}+K\,.\end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186068589 :question/id #uuid "3a2e21bb-c966-5429-98c0-9af209c45dfe" :question/math-academy-id "e-510" :question/problem "Evaluate $$ \displaystyle \int \dfrac{4x^2-x}{(x^2+x+1)(x-2)} \, \textrm{d}x. $$" :question/worked-solution "Notice that the quadratic factor in the denominator has a negative discriminant: $$ \mathcal{D} = 1^2 - 4(1)(1) = -3 < 0 $$ So, we proceed with the following partial fraction decomposition: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{4{x}^{2}-x}{({x}^{2}+x+1)(x-2)} & =\frac{Ax+B}{{x}^{2}+x+1}+\frac{C}{x-2}\end{aligned} $$ To determine the coefficients $A,$ $B,$ and $C,$ we first multiply both sides of the above equation by $(x^2+x+1)(x-2)$ and get $$ \begin{aligned}4{x}^{2}-x & =(Ax+B)(x-2)+C({x}^{2}+x+1).\end{aligned} $$ Solving for the unknown constants using the usual methods, we get $A=2,$ $B=1,$ and $C=2.$ Therefore, $$ \dfrac{4x^2-x}{(x^2+x+1)(x-2)} = \dfrac{2x+1}{x^2+x+1} + \dfrac{2}{x-2}. $$ Now we integrate this function term by term, adding the constant of integration only at the very end. $$ \begin{aligned}\int \frac{4{x}^{2}-x}{({x}^{2}+x+1)(x-2)}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{2x+1}{{x}^{2}+x+1}+\frac{2}{x-2})\text{d}x \\ & =\int \frac{2x+1}{{x}^{2}+x+1}\,\text{d}x+2\int \frac{1}{x-2}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned} $$ For the first integral, we use the substitution $u = x^2+x+1.$ Then $(2x+1) \, \textrm{d}x=\textrm{d}u,$ and we get $$ \begin{aligned}\int \frac{2x+1}{{x}^{2}+x+1}\,\text{d}x & =\int \left(\frac{1}{u}\right)\text{d}u \\ & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|u| \\ & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|{x}^{2}+x+1| \\ & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+x+1).\end{aligned} $$ For the second integral we have $$ \begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{x-2}\,\text{d}x & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-2|.\end{aligned} $$ So we get the following result: $$ \begin{aligned}\int \frac{4{x}^{2}-x}{({x}^{2}+x+1)(x-2)}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{2x+1}{{x}^{2}+x+1}\,\text{d}x+2\int \frac{1}{x-2}\,\text{d}x \\ & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+x+1)+2\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-2|+K\end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186068603 :question/id #uuid "f4e10cc3-f6f6-5cd8-b240-60417f37a021" :question/math-academy-id "e-5195" :question/problem "Find the point(s) of intersection of the curves $y=\sqrt {x+1}$ and $y=\dfrac{x}{2}+\dfrac{1}{2}$." :question/worked-solution "We need to solve the following system: $$ {\left\{ \begin{array}{l}y = \sqrt{x + 1} \\ y = {\displaystyle \frac{x}{2}} + {\displaystyle \frac{1}{2}}\end{array} \right. } $$ Setting the equations equal to one another and then solving for $x$, we get: $$ \begin{aligned} \sqrt{x + 1} &= \frac{x}{2} + \frac{1}{2} \\ x + 1 &= (\frac{x}{2} + \frac{1}{2})^{2} \\ x + 1 &= \frac{x^{2}}{4} + \frac{x}{2} + \frac{1}{4} \\ 4x + 4 &= x^{2} + 2x + 1 \\ x^{2} - 2x - 3 &= 0 \\ (x + 1)(x - 3) &= 0 \\ x &= -1, 3 \end{aligned} $$ Since we're dealing with square roots, we need to plug each of these solutions back into $$ \sqrt {x+1}=\dfrac{x}{2}+\dfrac{1}{2} $$ to check whether it satisfies the original equation. - For $x=-1$, we have $$ \begin{aligned}\sqrt{-1+1} & =\frac{-1}{2}+\frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & =0,\hspace{1em}{\color{green}{✓}}\end{aligned} $$ so $x=-1$ is indeed a solution of $\sqrt {x+1}=\dfrac{x}{2}+\dfrac{1}{2}$. - For $x=3$, we have $$ \begin{aligned}\sqrt{3+1} & =\frac{3}{2}+\frac{1}{2} \\ 2 & =2,\hspace{1em}{\color{green}{✓}}\end{aligned} $$ so $x=3$ is indeed a solution of $\sqrt {x+1}=\dfrac{x}{2}+\dfrac{1}{2}$. We found that both $x=-1$ and $x=3$ are solutions of $$ \sqrt {x+1}=\dfrac{x}{2}+\dfrac{1}{2} $$ To find the $y$-coordinates of the intersection points, we plug these values into either curve. Let's choose the radical curve, since it looks simpler. - Substituting $x=-1$, we get $$ \begin{aligned}y & =\sqrt{x+1} \\ & =\sqrt{-1+1} \\ & =\sqrt{0} \\ & =0,\end{aligned} $$ so one point of intersection is $(-1,0)$. - Substituting $x=3$, we get $$ \begin{aligned}y & =\sqrt{x+1} \\ & =\sqrt{3+1} \\ & =\sqrt{4} \\ & =2,\end{aligned} $$ so the other point of intersection is $(3,2)$. Therefore, we conclude that the points of intersection of the two curves are $(-1,0)$ and $(3,2)$. A sketch of the situation is shown below. ![](images/b4/b4444f4cbb83e5a9d55f6d654a25b7b79ff8a2f02dc6a36d290e5fdf1da42da2.png)"} {:db/id 17592186068609 :question/id #uuid "ff023940-30f8-5b30-ab1b-9ca1f335a6a8" :question/math-academy-id "e-553" :question/problem "Find the area of the finite region enclosed between $f(x) =x^2-2x+2$ and $g(x) = 2,$ shown below. ![](images/01/01f139c53b6328341b463f5ad941d37fccb241fff109c0584207017341e8e5f7.png)" :question/worked-solution "First, we want to determine the limits of integration. To do this, we equate the two functions and solve for $x\mathbin{:}$ $$ \begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-2x+2 & =2 \\ {x}^{2}-2x & =0 \\ x(x-2) & =0\end{aligned} $$ Hence, we need to integrate from $x=0$ to $x=2.$ To determine which is the lower function and which is the upper, we draw our vertical arrow. ![](images/39/39798ef4ff6e898527864628dc2750f88b115c03b2d6b8fb729f30b21d2d2bf5.png) The vertical line - *enters* the region through the lower function $y=x^2-2x+2,$ and - *leaves* through the upper function $y=2.$ Therefore, we can find the area as follows: $$ \begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{0}^{2}[\,(\text{upper function})-(\text{lower function})\,]\,\text{d}x \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{2}[\,(2)-({x}^{2}-2x+2)\,]\,\text{d}x \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(-{x}^{2}+2x)\,\text{d}x \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(2x-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\ & ={({x}^{2}-\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3})|}_{0}^{2} \\ & =({2}^{2}-\frac{1}{3}\cdot {2}^{3})-(0-0) \\ & =(4-\frac{8}{3})-0 \\ & =\frac{4}{3}\end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186068614 :question/id #uuid "8787186e-94bd-53da-9304-b0d3efbcb966" :question/math-academy-id "e-5823" :question/problem "Solve for $a$ where $$ \displaystyle \dfrac{2a -5}{3a^2} + \dfrac{1}{a} = \dfrac{a-1}{2a^2}. $$" :question/worked-solution "First, note that $a = 0$ cannot be a solution since division by $0$ is undefined. Now, let's multiply both sides of the equation by the least common denominator. The equation has the denominators $3a^2,$ $a,$ and $2a^2,$ so the least common multiple (or $\textrm{LCM}$) of the denominators is $$ \textrm{LCM}(3a^2, a, 2a^2) = 6a^2. $$ Multiplying both sides of the equation by $6a^2$ and simplifying, we get $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{2a-5}{3{a}^{2}}+\frac{1}{a} & =\frac{a-1}{2{a}^{2}} \\ 6{a}^{2}\cdot (\frac{2a-5}{3{a}^{2}}+\frac{1}{a}) & =6{a}^{2}\cdot \left(\frac{a-1}{2{a}^{2}}\right) \\ 6{a}^{2}\cdot \left(\frac{2a-5}{3{a}^{2}}\right)+6{a}^{2}\cdot \left(\frac{1}{a}\right) & =6{a}^{2}\cdot \left(\frac{a-1}{2{a}^{2}}\right) \\ 2\cdot 3{a}^{2}\cdot \left(\frac{2a-5}{3{a}^{2}}\right)+6a\cdot a\cdot \left(\frac{1}{a}\right) & =3\cdot 2{a}^{2}\cdot \left(\frac{a-1}{2{a}^{2}}\right) \\ 2\cdot \cancel{3{a}^{2}}\cdot \left(\frac{2a-5}{\cancel{3{a}^{2}}}\right)+6a\cdot \cancel{a}\cdot \left(\frac{1}{\cancel{a}}\right) & =3\cdot \cancel{2{a}^{2}}\cdot \left(\frac{a-1}{\cancel{2{a}^{2}}}\right) \\ 2\cdot (2a-5)+6a\cdot (1) & =3\cdot (a-1) \\ 2(2a-5)+6a & =3(a-1).\end{aligned} $$ We now have a linear equation in $a,$ and we can solve this using the addition and multiplication principles: $$ \begin{aligned}2(2a-5)+6a & =3(a-1) \\ 4a-10+6a & =3a-3 \\ 10a-10 & =3a-3 \\ 10a-3a & =-3+10 \\ 7a & =7 \\ a & =1\end{aligned} $$ Finally, recall that we cannot allow $a=0$ as a solution. Since $a=1$ is different from $a=0,$ we can accept it as a solution. Therefore, the solution is $a=1.$"} {:db/id 17592186068615 :question/id #uuid "84d3492d-12bb-50c2-b5b4-5f08567eb4f5" :question/math-academy-id "e-5825" :question/problem "Solve for $x$ where $$ \displaystyle 3 - \dfrac{10x+7}{8x} = \dfrac{6x-3}{2x}. $$" :question/worked-solution "First, note that $x=0$ cannot be a solution since division by $0$ is undefined. Now, let's multiply both sides of the equation by the least common denominator. The equation has the denominators $8x$ and $2x,$ so the least common multiple (or $\textrm{LCM}$) of the denominators is $$ \textrm{LCM}(8x,2x) = 8x. $$ Multiplying both sides of the equation by $8x$ and simplifying, we get $$ \begin{aligned}3-\frac{10x+7}{8x} & =\frac{6x-3}{2x} \\ 8x\cdot (3-\frac{10x+7}{8x}) & =8x\cdot \left(\frac{6x-3}{2x}\right) \\ 8x\cdot 3-8x\cdot \left(\frac{10x+7}{8x}\right) & =8x\cdot \left(\frac{6x-3}{2x}\right) \\ 24x-\cancel{8x}\cdot \left(\frac{10x+7}{\cancel{8x}}\right) & =4\cdot \cancel{2x}\cdot \left(\frac{6x-3}{\cancel{2x}}\right) \\ 24x-(10x+7) & =4\cdot (6x-3).\end{aligned} $$ We now have a linear equation in $x,$ and we can solve this using the addition and multiplication principles: $$ \begin{aligned}24x-(10x+7) & =4\cdot (6x-3) \\ 14x-7 & =24x-12 \\ 24x-14x & =-7+12 \\ 10x & =5 \\ x & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned} $$ Finally, recall that we cannot allow $x=0$ as a solution. Since $x= \dfrac 12$ is different from $x=0,$ we accept it as a solution. Therefore, the solution is $x= \dfrac 12.$"} {:db/id 17592186068617 :question/id #uuid "3a0a00c8-8a86-52de-bc9d-d9219a0735cf" :question/math-academy-id "e-591" :question/problem "![](images/73/7373418f2a0bac416e37662cea5a79101220820aa6f23c50a80fbf6addc5eefd.png) Consider the finite region bounded by $y=x^2$ and $y=x^5,$ as shown above. The equation has the denominators $x, 6x,$ and $3x,$ so the the least common multiple (or $\textrm{LCM}$) of the denominators is $$ \textrm{LCM}(x, 6x, 3x) = 6x. $$ Multiplying both sides of the equation by $6x$ and simplifying, we get $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{1+x}{x}+\frac{5+x}{6x} & =\frac{1-x}{3x} \\ 6x\cdot (\frac{1+x}{x}+\frac{5+x}{6x}) & =6x\cdot \frac{1-x}{3x} \\ 6x\cdot \left(\frac{1+x}{x}\right)+6x\cdot \left(\frac{5+x}{6x}\right) & =6x\cdot \left(\frac{1-x}{3x}\right) \\ 6x\cdot \left(\frac{1+x}{x}\right)+6x\cdot \left(\frac{5+x}{6x}\right) & =2\cdot 3x\cdot \left(\frac{1-x}{3x}\right) \\ 6\cancel{x}\cdot \left(\frac{1+x}{\cancel{x}}\right)+\cancel{6x}\cdot \left(\frac{5+x}{\cancel{6x}}\right) & =2\cdot \cancel{3x}\cdot \left(\frac{1-x}{\cancel{3x}}\right) \\ 6(1+x)+(5+x) & =2(1-x).\end{aligned} $$ We now have a linear equation in $x,$ and we can solve this using the addition and multiplication principles: $$ \begin{aligned}6(1+x)+(5+x) & =2(1-x) \\ 6+6x+5+x & =2-2x \\ 7x+11 & =2-2x \\ 7x+2x & =2-11 \\ 9x & =-9 \\ x & =-1\end{aligned} $$ Finally, recall that we cannot allow $x=0$ as a solution. Since $x=-1$ is different from $x=0,$ we can accept it as the solution. We'll work out the indefinite integral first, and then proceed to work out the definite integral. In this case, we define $$ \begin{aligned}u={t}^{2}+1\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t}=2t, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}={e}^{2t+1}\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t=\int {e}^{2t+1}\,\text{d}t=\frac{{e}^{2t+1}}{2}.\end{aligned} $$ Using the formula of integration by parts, we get $$ \begin{aligned}\int ({t}^{2}+1){e}^{2t+1}\,\text{d}t & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\ & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\ & =({t}^{2}+1)\left(\frac{{e}^{2t+1}}{2}\right)-\int \left(\frac{{e}^{2t+1}}{2}\right)(2t)\,\text{d}t \\ & =\frac{({t}^{2}+1){e}^{2t+1}}{2}-\int t\,{e}^{2t+1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned} $$ We use integration by parts once again to evaluate $$ \displaystyle\int t\,e^{2t+1}\,\textrm{d}t. $$ We take $$ \begin{aligned}u=t\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t}=1 \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}={e}^{2t+1}\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t=\int {e}^{2t+1}\,\text{d}t=\frac{{e}^{2t+1}}{2}.\end{aligned} $$ In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives $$ \begin{aligned}\int t\,{e}^{2t+1}\,\text{d}t & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\ & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\ & =(t)\left(\frac{{e}^{2t+1}}{2}\right)-\int \left(\frac{{e}^{2t+1}}{2}\right)(1)\,\text{d}t \\ & =\frac{t\,{e}^{2t+1}}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\int {e}^{2t+1}\,\text{d}t \\ & =\frac{t\,{e}^{2t+1}}{2}-\frac{{e}^{2t+1}}{4}+D,\end{aligned} $$ where $D$ is a constant. So, we get that the indefinite integral is $$ \begin{aligned}\int ({t}^{2}+1){e}^{2t+1}\,\text{d}t & =\frac{({t}^{2}+1){e}^{2t+1}}{2}-\int t\,{e}^{2t+1}\,\text{d}t \\ & =\frac{({t}^{2}+1){e}^{2t+1}}{2}-(\frac{t\,{e}^{2t+1}}{2}-\frac{{e}^{2t+1}}{4}+D) \\ & =\frac{({t}^{2}+1){e}^{2t+1}}{2}-\frac{t\,{e}^{2t+1}}{2}+\frac{{e}^{2t+1}}{4}-D \\ & =\frac{{e}^{2t+1}}{4}(2{t}^{2}-2t+3)+C,\end{aligned} $$ where $C = -{D}.$ Finally then, we can work out the definite integral: $$ \begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}({t}^{2}+1){e}^{2t+1}\,\text{d}t & ={[\frac{{e}^{2t+1}}{4}(2{t}^{2}-2t+3)]}_{0}^{1} \\ & =(\frac{{e}^{2(1)+1}}{4}(2(1)^{2}-2(1)+3))-(\frac{{e}^{2(0)+1}}{4}(2(0)^{2}-2(0)+3)) \\ & =\frac{{e}^{3}}{4}(2-2+3)-\frac{e}{4}(0-0+3) \\ & =\frac{3{e}^{3}}{4}-\frac{3e}{4} \\ & =\frac{3{e}^{3}-3e}{4}\end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186068638 :question/id #uuid "a25b6d87-7779-5408-90d6-a558baaae70f" :question/math-academy-id "e-7055" :question/problem "Consider the finite region bounded by the curve $x=2-y^2$ and the $y$-axis, as shown below. We find the intersections of the curve with the $y$-axis by solving for $y$ the following equation: $$ \begin{aligned} 2 - y^{2} &= 0 \\ y^{2} &= 2 \end{aligned} $$ Hence, the solutions are $$ y=\pm \sqrt 2 $$ So, we need to integrate from $$ y=-\sqrt{2} $$ to $$ y=\sqrt 2 $$ Finally, the volume can be found as follows: $$ \begin{aligned} V &= π\int_{c}^{d}[g(y)]^{2}dy \\ &= π\int_{-\sqrt{2}}^{\sqrt{2}}(2 - y^{2})^{2}dy \\ &= π\int_{-\sqrt{2}}^{\sqrt{2}}(4 - 4y^{2} + y^{4})dy \\ &= 2π\int_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}(4 - 4y^{2} + y^{4})dy \\ &= 2π[4y - \frac{4}{3}y^{3} + \frac{1}{5}y^{5}]_{0}^{\sqrt{2}} \\ &= 2π([4(\sqrt{2}) - \frac{4}{3}(\sqrt{2})^{3} + \frac{1}{5}(\sqrt{2})^{5}] - [0]) \\ &= 2π(4\sqrt{2} - \frac{8\sqrt{2}}{3} + \frac{4\sqrt{2}}{5}) \\ &= 2π\left(\frac{32\sqrt{2}}{15}\right) \\ &= \frac{64π\sqrt{2}}{15} \end{aligned} $$ **Note:** Since the region is symmetrical about the $x$-axis, in step $3$ above we were able to write $$ a sum of partial fractions: $$ \dfrac{x}{(x+1)^2} = \dfrac {A}{x+1} + \dfrac {B}{(x+1)^2} $$ To determine the coefficients $A$ and $B,$ we first multiply both sides of the above equation by $(x+1)^2$ and get $$ x= A(x+1)+B. $$ Plugging in $x=-1,$ we can eliminate $A$ and solve for $B\mathbin{:}$ $$ \begin{aligned}-1 & =A(-1+1)+B \\ B & =-1\end{aligned} $$ Now, plugging in $x=0$ and substituting the known value of $B,$ we can solve for $A\mathbin{:}$ $$ \begin{aligned}0 & =A(0+1)+B \\ 0 & =A+B \\ 0 & =A-1 \\ A & =1\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, we can write the integrand as the partial sum $$ \dfrac{x}{(x+1)^2} = \dfrac {1}{x+1} - \dfrac {1}{(x+1)^2}. $$ Finally, we integrate this expression term by term to get $$ \begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+2x+1}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{1}{x+1}-\frac{1}{(x+1)^{2}})\text{d}x \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{x+1}\,\text{d}x-{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{(x+1)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\ & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+1|{|}_{0}^{1}+{\frac{1}{x+1}|}_{0}^{1} \\ & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡|1+1|-\operatorname{ln}⁡|0+1|)+(\frac{1}{1+1}-\frac{1}{0+1}) \\ & \dfrac{3x^2-5x+8}{(x-3)^2(x+1)} = \dfrac{2}{(x-3)} +\dfrac{5}{(x-3)^2} +\dfrac{1}{(x+1)}. $$ Finally, we integrate this expression term by term, and get $$ \begin{aligned}\int To do that, we find the intersections of the curves by solving the following equation for $y:$ $$ \begin{aligned}f(y) & =g(y) \\ \sqrt{y} & ={y}^{3} \\ \sqrt{y}-{y}^{3} & =0 \\ \sqrt{y}\,(1-{y}^{5/2}) & =0\end{aligned} $$ Hence, the limits of integration are from $y=0$ and $y=1.$ Let's draw our horizontal arrow through the region to determine the inner function and the outer function. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation. ![](images/cd/cdf95299f8b925adcec743141bda4d94ad5542bfa8859fbdf5501ae0d56cd4e8.png) The horizontal arrow - *enters* the region through the inner function $x=g(y)={y}^{3},$ and - *leaves* through the outer function $x=f(y)=\sqrt{y}.$ Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is $$ \begin{aligned}V & =\pi {\int }_{a}^{b}([\text{outer}]^{2}-[\text{inner}]^{2})\text{d}y \\ & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({[\sqrt{y}]}^{2}-{[{y}^{3}]}^{2})\text{d}y \\ & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(y-{y}^{6})\text{d}y \\ & =\pi {(\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{y}^{7}}{7})|}_{0}^{1} \\ & =\pi [(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{7})-0] \\ & =\frac{5\pi }{14}.\end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186069016 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "31f4d92d-a272-589c-aaa2-26e10752eec6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{7\pi }{12}" :db/id 17592186528423} {:answer/id #uuid "4173c919-b0a7-54eb-a3f1-ef3e434be901" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{49\pi }{12}" :db/id 17592186528468} {:answer/id #uuid "600e3932-6193-582e-b8d3-9f02d1dac288" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{3}" :db/id 17592186528526} {:answer/id #uuid "9e4d79fc-2e5f-5cec-b5a4-479e429bcf09" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{5}" :db/id 17592186528679} {:answer/id #uuid "a1a21577-4501-5227-9e07-538c3f614cde" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{4\pi }{3}" :db/id 17592186528688}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186528526} :answer-field/id #uuid "607040d4-42b3-5cc5-ad6f-1ef6c33ab08e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186065529}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "0d8dce30-577d-5868-b247-3c35e51af095" :question/math-academy-id "q-11102" :question/problem "![](images/62/6250d388875796ad05e4d3eb8a5f625b6a633cbf0e9efb24926f72a9c6ceac7f.png) Consider the finite region bounded by $y=1-{x}^{2}$ and $x=1-\sqrt{y},$ as shown above. :question/worked-solution "First, we convert the integrand into a sum of partial fractions: $$ \frac{5x+35}{(x+2)^{2}(x-3)}=\frac{A}{(x+2)}+\frac{B}{(x+2)^{2}}+\frac{C}{(x-3)} $$ To determine the coefficients $A,$ $B,$ and $C,$ we first multiply both sides of the above equation by $(x+2)^{2}(x-3)$ and get $$ 5x+35=A(x+2)(x-3)+B(x-3)+C(x+2)^{2}. $$ Plugging in $x=-2,$ we can eliminate $A$ and $C$ and solve for $B:$ $$ \begin{aligned}5(-2)+35 & =A(-2+2)(-2-3)+B(-2-3)+C(-2+2)^{2} \\ -10+35 & =B(-5) \\ B & =\frac{25}{-5} \\ B & =-5\end{aligned} $$ Plugging in $x=3,$ we can eliminate $A$ and $B$ and solve for $C:$ $$ \begin{aligned}5(3)+35 & =A(3+2)(3-3)+B(3-3)+C(3+2)^{2} \\ 15+35 & =C{(5)}^{2} \\ C & =\frac{50}{25} \\ C & =2\end{aligned} $$ Plugging in $x=0$ and substituting the known values of $B$ and $C,$ we can solve for $A:$ $$ \begin{aligned}5(0)+35 & =A(0+2)(0-3)+B(0-3)+C(0+2)^{2} \\ 35 & =-6A-3B+4C \\ 35 & =-6A-3(-5)+4(2) \\ 35 & =-6A+23 \\ 6A & =-35+23 \\ A & =\frac{-12}{6} \\ A & =-2\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, $$ \frac{5x+35}{(x+2)^{2}(x-3)}=-\frac{2}{(x+2)}-\frac{5}{(x+2)^{2}}+\frac{2}{(x-3)}. $$ Finally, we integrate this expression term by term, and get $$ \begin{aligned}\int \frac{5x+35}{(x+2)^{2}(x-3)}\,\text{d}x & =\int (-\frac{2}{(x+2)}-\frac{5}{(x+2)^{2}}+\frac{2}{(x-3)})\,\text{d}x \\ & =-2\int \frac{1}{x+2}\,\text{d}x-5\int \frac{1}{(x+2)^{2}}\,\text{d}x+2\int \frac{1}{x-3}\,\text{d}x \\ & =-2\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+2|+\frac{5}{x+2}+2\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-3|+K,\end{aligned} $$ where $K$ is an integral constant."} {:db/id :question/worked-solution "We need to use integration by parts. In this case, we define $$ \begin{aligned}u=(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{2}\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x} \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}={x}^{2}\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x=\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}.\end{aligned} $$ Using the formula of integration by parts, we get $$ \begin{aligned}\int {x}^{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\ & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\ & ={(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}\left(\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}\right)-\int \left(\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}\right)\left(\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x}\right)\,\text{d}x \\ & =\frac{{x}^{3}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}}{3}-\frac{2}{3}\int {x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned} $$ We use integration by parts once again to evaluate $$ \displaystyle \int {x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x. $$ We take $$ \begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x} \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}={x}^{2}\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x=\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}.\end{aligned} $$ In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives $$ \begin{aligned}\int {x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\ & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\ & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x))\left(\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}\right)-\int \left(\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}\right)\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)\,\text{d}x \\ & =\frac{{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}{3}-\frac{1}{3}\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\ & =\frac{{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}{3}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{9}+D,\end{aligned} $$ where $D$ is an integral constant. So we have $$ \begin{aligned}\int {x}^{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{{x}^{3}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}}{3}-\frac{2}{3}(\frac{{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}{3}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{9}+D) \\ & =\frac{{x}^{3}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}}{3}-\frac{2{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}{9}+\frac{2{x}^{3}}{27}-\frac{2D}{3} \\ & =\frac{{x}^{3}}{27}(9(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{2}-6\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)+2)+C,\end{aligned} $$ where $C=-\frac{2D}{3}.$"} {:db/id 17592186069042 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices In this case, we define $$ \begin{aligned}u={\ln }^{2}⁡(x)\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}{x} \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x=-\frac{1}{2{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned} $$ Using the formula of integration by parts, we get $$ \begin{aligned}\int \frac{{\ln }^{2}⁡x}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\text{d}x \\ & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\ & =({\ln }^{2}⁡(x))\left(-\frac{1}{2{x}^{2}}\right)-\int \left(-\frac{1}{2{x}^{2}}\right)\left(\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}{x}\right)\,\text{d}x \\ & =-\frac{{\ln }^{2}⁡(x)}{2{x}^{2}}+\int \frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned} $$ We use integration by parts once again to evaluate $$ \displaystyle \int \frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}{{x}^{3}}\text{d}x. $$ We take $$ \begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x} \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x=-\frac{1}{2{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned} $$ In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives $$ \begin{aligned}\int \frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\ & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\ & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x))\left(-\frac{1}{2{x}^{2}}\right)-\int \left(-\frac{1}{2{x}^{2}}\right)\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)\,\text{d}x \\ & =-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}{2{x}^{2}}+\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x \\ & =-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}{2{x}^{2}}-\frac{1}{4{x}^{2}}+C,\end{aligned} $$ where $C$ is an integral constant. So we have $$ \begin{aligned}\int \frac{{\ln }^{2}⁡x}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x & =-\frac{{\ln }^{2}⁡(x)}{2{x}^{2}}+(-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}{2{x}^{2}}-\frac{1}{4{x}^{2}}+C) \\ & =-\frac{{\ln We find that $$ \text{LCM}(36b,12{b}^{2})=36{b}^{2}. $$ So, we multiply both sides of the equation by $36{b}^{2},$ and simplify: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{5b+8}{12{b}^{2}} & =-\frac{12}{36b}+\frac{4b+8}{12{b}^{2}} \\ 36{b}^{2}\cdot \left(\frac{5b+8}{12{b}^{2}}\right) & =36{b}^{2}\cdot (-\frac{12}{36b}+\frac{4b+8}{12{b}^{2}}) \\ 36{b}^{2}\cdot \left(\frac{5b+8}{12{b}^{2}}\right) & =36{b}^{2}\cdot \left(-\frac{12}{36b}\right)+36{b}^{2}\cdot \left(\frac{4b+8}{12{b}^{2}}\right) \\ 3\cdot 12{b}^{2}\cdot \left(\frac{5b+8}{12{b}^{2}}\right) & =b\cdot 36b\cdot \left(-\frac{12}{36b}\right)+3\cdot 12{b}^{2}\cdot \left(\frac{4b+8}{12{b}^{2}}\right) \\ 3\cdot \cancel{12{b}^{2}}\cdot \left(\frac{5b+8}{\cancel{12{b}^{2}}}\right) & =b\cdot \cancel{36b}\cdot \left(-\frac{12}{\cancel{36b}}\right)+3\cdot \cancel{12{b}^{2}}\cdot \left(\frac{4b+8}{\cancel{12{b}^{2}}}\right) \\ 3(5b+8) & =-12b+3(4b+8)\end{aligned} $$ We now have a linear equation in $b,$ and we can solve this using the addition and multiplication principles: $$ \begin{aligned}3(5b+8) & =-12b+3(4b+8) \\ 15b+24 & =-12b+12b+24 \\ 15b+24 & =24 \\ 15b & =24-24 \\ 15b & =0 \\ b & =0\end{aligned} $$ Finally, we recall that we cannot allow $b=0$ as a solution. $$ D=(-6)^{2}-4(2)(9)=-36<0 $$ So, we proceed with the following partial fraction decomposition: $$ \frac{15-25x}{(2{x}^{2}-6x+9)(x-4)}=\frac{Ax+B}{2{x}^{2}-6x+9}+\frac{C}{x-4} $$ To determine the coefficients $A,B,$ and $C,$ we first multiply both sides of the above equation by $(2{x}^{2}-6x+9)(x-4),$ and we get $$ 15-25x=(Ax+B)(x-4)+C(2{x}^{2}-6x+9). $$ Solving for the unknown constants using the usual methods, we get $A=10,B=-15$ and $C=-5.$ Therefore, $$ \frac{15-25x}{(2{x}^{2}-6x+9)(x-4)}=\frac{10x-15}{2{x}^{2}-6x+9}+\frac{-5}{x-4}. $$ We now integrate this function term by term, adding the constant of integration at the very end. $$ \begin{aligned}\int \frac{15-25x}{(2{x}^{2}-6x+9)(x-4)}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{10x-15}{2{x}^{2}-6x+9}+\frac{-5}{x-4})\,\text{d}x \\ & =5\int \frac{2x-3}{2{x}^{2}-6x+9}\,\text{d}x-5\int \frac{1}{x-4}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned} $$ For the first integral, we use the substitution $u=2{x}^{2}-6x+9.$ Then $\text{d}u=(4x-6)\,\text{d}x,$ and we get First, we note that a denominator of the integrand can be factored as $$ {x}^{2}-16=(x+4)(x-4). $$ So the integrand can be converted into a sum of partial fractions, $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{3x+4}{{x}^{2}-16} & =\frac{3x+4}{(x+4)(x-4)}=\frac{A}{(x+4)}+\frac{B}{(x-4)},\end{aligned} $$ which gives $$ 3x+4=A(x-4)+B(x+4). $$ Plugging in $x=4,$ we can eliminate $A$ and solve for $B:$ $$ \begin{aligned}3(4)+4 & =A(4-4)+B(4+4) \\ 16 & =8B \\ B & =2\end{aligned} $$ On the other hand, plugging in $x=-4,$ we can eliminate $B$ and solve for $A:$ $$ \begin{aligned}3(-4)+4 & =A(-4-4)+B(-4+4) \\ -8 & =-8A \\ A & =1\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, $$ \frac{3x+4}{{x}^{2}-16}=\frac{1}{(x+4)}+\frac{2}{(x-4)}. $$ Now, we integrate, and we get $$ \begin{aligned}\int \frac{3x+4}{{x}^{2}-16}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{1}{(x+4)}+\frac{2}{(x-4)})\,\text{d}x \\ & =\int \frac{1}{x+4}\,\text{d}x+2{\int }_{2}^{3}\frac{1}{x-4}\,\text{d}x \\ & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+4|+2\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-4|+C.\end{aligned} $$ We can simplify the result using the laws of logarithms, as follows: $$ \begin{aligned}\int \frac{3x+4}{{x}^{2}-16}\,\text{d}x & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+4|+2\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-4|+C \\ & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+4|+\operatorname{ln}⁡|(x-4)^{2}|+C \\ & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|(x+4)(x-4)^{2}|+C\end{aligned} $$ Finally, the definite integral is $$ \begin{aligned}{\int }_{2}^{3}\frac{3x+4}{{x}^{2}-16}\,\text{d}x & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|(x+4)(x-4)^{2}|{|}_{2}^{3} \\ & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(7)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(24) \\ & =\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{7}{24}\right).\end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186069397 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "18cf8091-e95f-5a3e-91c9-637550a5d656" true :question/worked-solution "The quadratic factor ${x}^{2}+1$ is irreducible, so we proceed with the following partial fraction decomposition: $$ \frac{2}{(x-1)({x}^{2}+1)}=\frac{A}{x-1}+\frac{Bx+C}{{x}^{2}+1}. $$ To determine the coefficients $A,B,$ and $C,$ we first multiply both sides of the above equation by $(x-1)({x}^{2}+1),$ and we get $$ 2=A({x}^{2}+1)+(Bx+C)(x-1). $$ Solving for the unknown constants using the usual methods, we get $A=1,B=-1,$ and $C=-1.$ Therefore, $$ \frac{2}{(x-1)({x}^{2}+1)}=\frac{1}{x-1}+\frac{-x-1}{{x}^{2}+1}. $$ We now integrate this function term by term, adding the constant of integration at the very end. $$ \begin{aligned}\int \frac{2}{(x-1)({x}^{2}+1)}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{1}{x-1}+\frac{-x-1}{{x}^{2}+1})\,\text{d}x \\ & =\int \frac{1}{x-1}\,\text{d}x-\int \frac{x}{{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x-\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned} $$ For the first integral, we have $$ \int \frac{1}{x-1}\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-1|. $$ For the second integral, we use the substitution $u={x}^{2}+1.$ Then $\text{d}u=2x\,\text{d}x,$ and we get $$ \begin{aligned}\int \frac{x}{{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x & =\int \left(\frac{1}{u}\right)\frac{\text{d}u}{2} \\ & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|u| \\ & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|{x}^{2}+1| \\ & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)\,.\end{aligned} $$ Finally, for the third integral, we use the fact that $$ \displaystyle \int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{a}^{2}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{a}\operatorname{arctan}⁡\left(\frac{x}{a}\right), $$ which results in $$ \int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{arctan}⁡x. $$ So, we get the following result: $$ \begin{aligned}\int \frac{2}{(x-1)({x}^{2}+1)}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{x-1}\,\text{d}x-\int \frac{x}{{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x-\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x \\ & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-1|-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)-\operatorname{arctan}⁡x+K\end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id We find that $$ \text{LCM}(x,2x,4x)=4x. $$ So, we multiply both sides of the equation by $4x,$ and simplify: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{1}{x} & =\frac{2+x}{2x}+\frac{3}{4x} \\ 4x\cdot \left(\frac{1}{x}\right) & =4x\cdot (\frac{2+x}{2x}+\frac{3}{4x}) \\ 4x\cdot \left(\frac{1}{x}\right) & =4x\cdot \left(\frac{2+x}{2x}\right)+4x\cdot \left(\frac{3}{4x}\right) \\ 4x\cdot \left(\frac{1}{x}\right) & =2\cdot 2x\cdot \left(\frac{2+x}{2x}\right)+4x\cdot \left(\frac{3}{4x}\right) \\ 4\cancel{x}\cdot \left(\frac{1}{\cancel{x}}\right) & =2\cdot \cancel{2x}\cdot \left(\frac{2+x}{\cancel{2x}}\right)+\cancel{4x}\cdot \left(\frac{3}{\cancel{4x}}\right) \\ 4\cdot (1) & =2\cdot (2+x)+3 \\ 4 & =2(2+x)+3\end{aligned} $$ We now have a linear equation in $x,$ and we can solve this using the addition and multiplication principles: $$ \begin{aligned}4 & =2(2+x)+3 \\ 4 & =4+2x+3 \\ 2x & =-3 \\ x & =-\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned} $$ Finally, we recall that we cannot allow $x=0$ as a solution.
